title: A game coin balance
summary: Store 20 starting coins and 7 spent coins. Calculate and print the coins left.
explanation: A program is a list of instructions the computer follows. A value is one piece of information, such as the number 30 or the text "coins". Numbers have no quotation marks here. Quotation marks tell JavaScript that the characters inside are text, also called a string. This project uses numbers so it can subtract an amount spent from an amount available.

A variable gives a value a name. In `const savedCoins = 30;`, `const` creates a name that cannot later be assigned a different value. `savedCoins` is the name, and the single equals sign `=` assigns the value on its right. A name cannot contain spaces or begin with a digit. JavaScript distinguishes capital and small letters: `savedCoins` and `savedcoins` are different names. The semicolon ends this instruction.

`console.log()` is a function used to display information. A function is a reusable action; calling it asks it to run. The dot in `console.log` selects the `log` action belonging to `console`. Parentheses `()` contain the value you want to display. Put the variable name inside, without quotes, to display its value. `console.log("coinsLeft")` instead displays the literal word coinsLeft because the quotes make it text.

Assignment and comparison ask different things. `const balance = 22;` assigns a value. `balance === 22` asks whether the value is exactly equal to 22 and produces `true` or `false`. Those are Boolean values, the two possible answers to a yes-or-no question. The minus sign subtracts; the plus sign adds numbers; the star `*` multiplies numbers. Choose the sign that matches the action you mean.

For your project, calculate with the supplied variable names so the calculation follows their values. The supplied amounts give 20 minus 7, which is 13. A second run with spending changed to 5 gives 15. Trace each line: which two values go into the expression, what number comes out, and which name is printed? Storing a number and displaying it are separate steps, and the checks look at both.

analogy.familiar: A labeled place on a score sheet
analogy.connection: The name helps you refer to the current number.
analogy.limit: A variable is not always a separate box in computer memory. Objects can be shared through names, and const prevents reassignment of the name but does not freeze every object value.

steps: Use the supplied values: startingCoins is 20 and spentCoins is 7.
Replace the TODO value with startingCoins minus spentCoins.
Print remainingCoins with console.log.
Run the checks, then change spentCoins to 5 and predict the new output.

checks.label: The named values produce the correct balance.

quiz.explanation: The minus sign subtracts 7 from 20. console.log displays the result, 13.

math.explanation: Subtraction finds how much remains after some coins are spent.

title: A page about your favorite place
summary: Add a heading, a short paragraph, a link, and an image.
explanation:
A web page starts with content: words, pictures, and actions. HTML means HyperText Markup Language. “Markup” means adding labels around content so a browser knows what each part means. A browser is the program that opens a website. An HTML element is a whole piece, such as a heading together with its tags. In

Hello!

,

starts a paragraph, Hello! is the content, and

ends it. The slash means “this element ends here.” HTML names meaning and structure; colors and spacing are usually CSS's job.

This is a complete small HTML document. Save it as index.html and open it in a browser. ```html Mountain lookout

Mountain lookout

I like watching the clouds drift past.

``` The first line asks for modern HTML behavior. html wraps the document; lang="en" says its language is English, which helps tools read it aloud. head holds information about the page. title names the browser tab. body holds the visible content. h1 gives the main heading, and p gives the paragraph. meta provides a document setting. charset="utf-8" tells the browser to interpret the file using UTF-8, a character encoding that can represent letters and symbols from many languages.

The angle brackets < and > mark tags. An attribute is an extra setting inside an opening tag. In lang="en", lang is the attribute name and "en" is its value. The equals sign connects them; quotes mark where the value starts and ends. Nesting means putting one element inside another. In the example, h1 and p are inside body. Close the inside element before closing its parent:

Text

. Indenting each nested level makes this relationship easier to see. Indentation helps people; it does not choose the tag's meaning.

An anchor, written a, makes a link. Its href attribute holds the destination address. The visible words between and tell readers what they will open. These jobs are different: changing the words does not change the address. Use useful words such as “Read the park guide,” rather than “Click here.” A full address such as https://example.org/lookout includes a scheme, https, and a site name. A local filename can also be a destination. The destination still needs to exist; making a link does not create the other page.

These two elements can go inside body, after the paragraph in the first example. ```html Read the lookout guide ``` Clicking the link asks the browser to open the href address. src means the image's source: the file or address from which to load it. This example needs a real lookout.jpg file beside index.html. img is a void element, meaning it has no content between opening and closing tags, so it needs no . The attributes still belong to its opening tag even when they use separate lines.

Alt text is a written replacement for an image's useful information. It can help when the picture fails to load or when someone uses a screen reader, a tool that speaks or presents page content in another way. Describe the information that matters here, rather than writing “image” or repeating a filename. A decorative image that adds no information normally gets alt="". This project's image is informative, so give it a useful description. A long description can pass a length check while still being unhelpful; read your own words and ask what a person would learn from them.

Before the project, predict what happens if you change href but keep the link words: the destination changes while the words stay the same. Now predict changing alt: the image file stays the same, while its written description changes. For the exercise, keep a main heading and add a short p, an a whose href is exactly https://example.org/trail, and an img with descriptive alt text. Check that all four parts exist, then actually follow the link and inspect the picture. The automatic checks can find the elements and address; they cannot judge whether your description matches the real image.

analogy.familiar: A small poster with title, note, directions and picture
analogy.connection: Tags label the job of each page part
analogy.limit: A label does not make a link useful unless its destination is correct.

Add an image with useful alt text.

quiz.explanation: href stores the destination; visible link words tell the reader what to expect.

title: A two-page hobby guide
summary: Create a home page and a supplies page with a list. Link the pages to each other.
explanation: A website can contain several HTML documents. Each document is a separate file, even when the pages look similar. A link joins them by giving the browser a path. A path tells it where to look for a file. index.html is often the name of the starting page; it is still an ordinary HTML file. Putting another filename in a paragraph only shows those words. To make navigation, put the filename in an a element's href. The destination file must exist at that location, and the spelling must match.

Save this example as index.html. It is a complete home page for a different hobby. ```html Paper models

Paper models

Build small houses from paper.

See the materials list ``` The h1 names the visible page. p adds an ordinary paragraph. a wraps the useful link words, and href="materials.html" asks for a file beside this page. The address is relative: the browser works it out using the current page's location.

A relative path starts from a known location instead of naming a whole website. materials.html means “look in the same folder.” images/fold.jpg means “open the images folder, then find fold.jpg.” ../index.html means “move up one folder, then find index.html.” A full address such as https://example.org/models starts with a scheme and site name. File names can be case sensitive on a web server: Materials.html and materials.html may differ. Spaces and accidentally changed extensions also cause broken links. Follow the actual file names, rather than guessing from the page's heading.

A list groups related items. ul means unordered list: the order is not meant to be a sequence of steps, and browsers usually show bullets. ol means ordered list: the order matters, and browsers usually show numbers. Each list entry goes inside li, meaning list item. Put li elements inside ul or ol, then close each li before starting another. Do not use paragraphs with typed bullet characters when you mean a real list. List elements let browsers and assistive tools recognize how many entries belong together.

Save this second complete document as materials.html beside index.html. ```html Model materials

Materials

  • Thick paper
  • Glue stick
Back to paper models
``` main identifies the main content. ul contains two li children. The return link points to the first file, so navigation works in both directions. Both links need their destination files; neither link creates a document.

HTML is nested. The second page's list is inside main, and its items are inside ul. Closing ends the list, so the following a is outside that list. Most of these elements use opening and closing tags. The slash closes an element; it is not part of a file path here. Attributes go in opening tags, and their values go in quotes. Read this code from the outside inward if you lose your place: html contains body, body contains main, and main contains the heading, list, and link.

For the project, keep the home heading exactly Garden journal and keep its paragraph. Add a useful link whose href is supplies.html. The supplied supplies.html already has its list and its link back to index.html; inspect it so you can explain both directions. Open the home page, follow the supplies link, and follow the return link. A check can confirm that the home anchor exists and has words, but that alone does not prove both files open. If navigation fails, compare the href with the actual filename and folder first.

analogy.connection: A link gives the browser a path between files
analogy.limit: The second file must exist in the project.

title: A clear event page
summary: Use meaningful sections for the title, navigation, main content, and footer.
explanation: Semantic HTML uses element names to say what content is for. Semantic means “about meaning.” A header introduces a page or section. nav holds a group of navigation links. main identifies the central content of the page. footer holds closing or supporting information. These names help someone understand the page without relying on how it looks. A browser may not visibly style them differently. Their meaning remains useful to assistive tools and to people reading your code. Choose them for their job, then use CSS later to choose appearance.

This complete page gives an event clear regions. ```html Science afternoon

Science afternoon

Experiments

Sunday at the community center.

Experiments

Try making a paper helicopter.

Adults and children are welcome.

``` header contains the event title. nav gives a shortcut to a section. One main holds the event details, and footer finishes the page.

A landmark is a page region that assistive tools can help people find quickly. main and nav provide meaningful landmarks. For this ordinary page, use one visible main content region. Put the site's repeated navigation outside it so “go to main content” leads to the details, rather than repeated links. aria-label adds a short accessible name to a region or control. Here “Event sections” helps explain the navigation's purpose; it does not add a visible heading. Keep the visible link words clear as well. Native semantic elements usually provide the role without extra role attributes.

Headings describe an outline. h1 names this page's main subject. h2 names a section within that subject; h3 can name a subsection inside an h2 section. Choose levels for the relationship between ideas, rather than for the text size you want. In this event, an h1 followed by an h2 makes that relationship simple. A section groups related content and usually has a heading. A div is a general container with no special meaning; use it when you need grouping without claiming a more specific role.

This fragment belongs inside a main element. A link elsewhere on the page can use href="#tickets" to reach it. ```html

Tickets

Admission is free.

Group visits

Tell the organizer how many people are coming.

``` id="tickets" gives the outer section a unique identifier. The # in a link destination means an in-page fragment, a named place inside the current document. h3 is nested beneath the Tickets topic. Close the inner section before the outer section. Indentation makes the hierarchy visible, while tags define the real structure.

An anchor's href and a target's id must match exactly. href="#experiments" finds id="experiments"; a heading with the same visible word but no matching id is not that target. IDs should be unique within a document. Links need useful words, and the link should lead to relevant content. A correct landmark does not repair confusing writing or a broken target. Review the page's reading order from top to bottom, because that order is also important when someone listens to the page or moves through it with a keyboard.

For the exercise, put the event's h1 inside header, name nav with aria-label, put the Schedule link in it, and use one main for details. Put an h2 in the schedule section and give the section id="schedule" so href="#schedule" works. Finish with footer. The checks look for these regions and heading levels; they do not prove the whole outline or reading order is sensible. Ask yourself what someone would learn by reading only the headings, then follow the Schedule link and check that its destination exists.

analogy.familiar: A flyer with named areas
analogy.connection: Semantic elements identify what each region is for
analogy.limit: Good structure alone does not make writing clear.

title: A page usable without a mouse
summary: Give images useful descriptions and controls clear names. Check every action with the keyboard.
explanation: Accessibility means making content and actions usable by people with different ways of seeing, hearing, moving, and understanding. Someone might use a keyboard, a screen reader, a touch screen, or a large zoom setting. Your HTML should still tell them what is there and what each control does. Start with built-in elements that already have useful behavior. A button is an action control; an a with href is a navigation link. Their meaning helps a browser and assistive tools offer the right interaction.

This is a complete example with an informative image and a named control. ```html Bike repair day

Bike repair day

``` The image requires a repair.jpg file. alt describes its useful information. The button has visible words that explain its purpose. This HTML creates the control; it does not yet supply code to open repair times.

An image's src tells the browser which picture to load. alt gives a text replacement. Imagine someone cannot see this picture: what information would they miss? Write that information in ordinary words. You usually do not need “picture of,” because the tool can already announce that it is an image. Decorative pictures that add no information normally have alt="". Do not leave alt out and assume that is the same: some tools may announce the file name. img has no closing tag because it is a void element, with no content inside it.

A control's accessible name is the name assistive tools use to identify it. For an ordinary button, its visible text supplies that name. Clear visible text helps everyone. Prefer “View repair times” to “Go” when the action would otherwise be unclear. type="button" makes it a plain button; inside a form, this avoids accidentally submitting the form. A native button can receive keyboard focus and can be activated using normal keyboard controls. A div with button-like styling does not automatically gain those behaviors.

This fragment belongs inside body and demonstrates navigation beside an action control. ```html Read directions to the workshop ``` The link needs a directions.html page and navigates to it. The button needs behavior added later if it should show a checklist. The small dot is decorative, so its empty alt lets assistive tools skip it. These choices depend on each element's purpose, not on its color or shape. Do not copy empty alt onto a picture that teaches useful information.

Keyboard focus marks the control that will receive a keyboard action. Press Tab to move forward through focusable controls and Shift+Tab to move backward. Check that you can see where focus is. A focused button should be usable with Enter or Space; a link normally activates with Enter. tabindex="-1" removes an element from normal Tab navigation, so it is not a way to make this exercise's button easy to reach. Keep the source order sensible and keep visible focus styling. These are useful checks, but they do not cover every accessibility need.

For the picnic exercise, add alt text that describes the informative image and give the native button the exact visible name View picnic details. Keep it keyboard focusable. Tab to it, check its name, and inspect focus. The automated checks verify text and basic focusability; the starter does not add the actual details-opening behavior. A button passing the naming check can still do nothing when activated. To judge a finished interactive page, test the real action, review images in context, and use a screen reader as well as the keyboard.

analogy.familiar: A door people need to find and open
analogy.connection: Clear names and keyboard focus make controls easier to use
analogy.limit: A keyboard check is not a complete accessibility test.

Give the button a name that says what it does.
Keep the native button element.
Tab to it and inspect the result.

title: An activity signup form
summary: Add labeled name, email, and activity fields with a submit button.
explanation: A form collects related choices or information. The form element groups its controls. An input is a single entry field; a select offers choices; a button can submit the form. A label tells a person what a control asks for. Controls need meaningful names even before someone types anything. A placeholder inside a field disappears while typing and should not replace its label. HTML can ask the browser to catch simple missing or malformed values, but saving information needs additional behavior and another system to receive it.

This form fragment belongs inside body. It demonstrates a labeled required field.

```html
<form>
  <label for="visitor">Visitor name</label>
  <input id="visitor" name="visitor" type="text" required>

  <label for="contact">Contact email</label>
  <input id="contact" name="contact" type="email" required>

  <button type="submit">Request information</button>
</form>
```

The label's for value matches the input's id exactly. Clicking a label can move focus to its connected field. input is a void element and needs no closing tag. required is a Boolean attribute: its presence turns the requirement on. Do not write required="false" to turn it off; remove it instead.

id and name have different jobs. An id identifies one element on the page, so use a unique id for each control. A label's for points to that id. name supplies the field's key when a form sends values, such as contact=someone@example.org. Matching a label to a control does not require matching name, but submitted controls generally need name. Attribute values belong inside quotes, and settings go in the opening tag. Keep labels next to the fields they describe so the visual order also makes sense.

type="email" tells the browser to check the shape of an email address when the form is submitted. It may also offer an email-friendly keyboard. required tells the browser that the field cannot be blank. Together they cover different problems: empty input and an address with the wrong shape. They do not prove that an address exists or belongs to the person. A server, the system receiving submitted information, still needs its own validation. Client-side validation means checks in the browser; it helps people correct errors but can be bypassed.

This fragment is another form, using a list of choices. Put it in body to try it separately.

```html
<form>
  <label for="session">Choose a session</label>
  <select id="session" name="session">
    <option value="music">Music</option>
    <option value="clay">Clay modeling</option>
  </select>
  <button type="submit">Choose session</button>
</form>
```

select contains option elements. Music is the visible option text; value="music" is the value sent if that option is selected. option and select use closing tags. The label connects to session just as it connects to an input. A submit button asks the browser to submit its form after eligible validation checks.

Try three kinds of input before trusting a form: missing, malformed, and valid. For a required email field, submit it empty, then enter a clearly malformed address, then an address-shaped example such as learner@example.org. Notice the different results. Native validation messages and appearance depend on the browser and its language. A form without a real receiving endpoint does not enroll someone or store their information. You can learn labeling and validation here without claiming that submission has connected to a registration service.

For this project, use controls with id="name", id="email", and id="activity", each connected to a visible label. Require name and email; set email's type to email. Use select with options for the activity and a submit button. Each label's for must exactly match its control's id. The checks find those relationships and attributes. Then try the blank and malformed cases yourself. Good form instructions should tell a person how to fix a problem without clearing their other answers or making them guess which field needs attention.

analogy.familiar: A paper registration card with named blanks
analogy.connection: Labels tell people what each input is for
analogy.limit: Browser checks do not replace server validation.

title: A multi-step registration form
summary: Build grouped form fields with native validation and helpful errors.
explanation: A longer form becomes easier to understand when related fields have clear groups. fieldset groups controls, and legend names the group. Contact details and account details are different subjects, so they can use separate fieldsets in one form. People using assistive tools can receive the group name with the fields. Grouping does not save information or guarantee that an answer is correct. It makes the form's structure clearer. This exercise builds grouped registration fields; showing one step at a time would require additional navigation behavior.

This fragment belongs inside body. It creates one labeled group with native validation.

```html
<form>
  <fieldset>
    <legend>Participant details</legend>
    <label for="participant">Participant name</label>
    <input id="participant" name="participant" required>

    <label for="reply">Reply email</label>
    <input id="reply" name="reply" type="email" required>
  </fieldset>
  <button type="submit">Continue</button>
</form>
```

legend is the first child of fieldset and names the group. Each label points to a unique input id. required asks for an answer, and type="email" checks an address-shaped value. The input elements need no closing tags, while form, fieldset, legend, label, and button do.

Constraints are limits on acceptable input. required rejects a missing answer during ordinary submission. type="email" adds a format check. minlength sets a minimum text length. These work together, rather than replacing each other. A minlength field that is optional can still be empty, so add required when empty input should be rejected. type="password" hides entered characters visually; it does not by itself encrypt, store, or secure the value. Any real account system needs separate secure handling and server validation.

Helpful instructions appear before someone makes an error. Tell them the length requirement in words near the field. A small element marks side information such as a short note, not a particular font size you must rely on. aria-describedby can connect a control to explanatory text through that text's id. Unlike a label, the description gives extra help rather than naming the field. Keep the actual visible label. IDs must be unique, and both for and aria-describedby must point to the correct elements.

Add this fieldset inside the same form, before its submit button, to give the example a second group.

```html
<fieldset>
  <legend>Account details</legend>
  <label for="secret">Passphrase</label>
  <input
    id="secret"
    name="secret"
    type="password"
    minlength="10"
    required
    aria-describedby="secret-help"
  >
  <small id="secret-help">Use at least ten characters.</small>
</fieldset>
```

The multi-line opening input tag is still one tag. The minimum here is ten, to show a different example. aria-describedby points to the help note. Nest this fieldset within form, and close it before the form closes.

Validate the paths someone can take. First submit with required fields blank. Next try an invalid email and a short passphrase. Then type valid-shaped information that meets the length rule. Browser validation normally prevents the ordinary submission while a participating field is invalid, and may focus it with a message. Test with typing, because programmatically changing values can behave differently for some constraints. Do not use a fake error that only says “Wrong”: say which field needs attention and what would make it acceptable. Native checks remain only part of a complete registration system.

For the workshop exercise, make exactly two fieldsets, each with a legend. Add labeled inputs for name, email, and passphrase, using the expected ids name, email, and pass. Require the needed fields, give email its email type, and give pass a minlength of at least eight. Keep a submit button. The checks verify groups, labels, and key constraints; they do not implement multi-step navigation or a database. Explain what each fieldset contains and test missing, invalid, and valid values with the keyboard before considering the form usable.

analogy.connection: Fieldsets group related controls; legends name the groups
analogy.limit: A form does not send or safely store data by itself.

title: A long-form guide
summary: Organize a guide with navigation, headings, tables, and meaningful landmarks.
explanation: A long guide needs ways to find information and understand how pieces relate. Use a main heading for the whole guide, section headings for its topics, and navigation links for shortcuts. Meaningful page regions are also called landmarks because assistive tools can help people move among them. Tables are for information whose rows and columns have relationships, such as each trail and its distance. They should not be used just to place unrelated page content side by side. A clear reading order helps both sighted readers and people listening to the guide.

This complete example gives a short guide a working in-page shortcut. ```html Bird guide
Bird list

Neighborhood birds

Birds near the pond

Look quietly from the path.

``` The #birds address finds id="birds". nav's aria-label names its purpose. One main marks the central content, h1 names the guide, and h2 names a topic inside it.

A table is built from nested elements. table wraps the whole thing. caption names what the table is about. tr means table row. th means header cell, which labels a row or column. td means an ordinary data cell. thead groups header rows; tbody groups the body rows. These tags describe relationships; a border alone cannot explain them. A table can have several cells in each row, and their order should match the header order. Close every cell before closing its row, then close the row group before closing table.

scope="col" on a th says it labels its column. scope="row" can mark a header for its row. The caption names the table as a whole, while column headers tell readers what each value means. “Name” and “Wingspan” explain separate columns. A person listening to a table may need the header repeated to understand a value, so use real th elements rather than bold ordinary cells. Simple scope-based headers are useful here; complex tables with multiple overlapping header groups need more careful relationships and testing.

Put this table inside the birds section from the first example. ```html
Bird wingspans
Bird Wingspan
Mallard 85 cm
Great blue heron 180 cm
``` The caption introduces the information. The first header applies to bird names, and the second applies to measurements. Each data row follows that same two-cell pattern. These example values are content, not code instructions.

Reading order comes from the document's structure. Keep headings, explanatory text, and the matching table together so the guide makes sense in order. Test navigation using Tab and Enter, and check that shortcuts lead to real sections. Use a screen reader to listen to the landmarks, headings, table caption, and column relationships. Automated checks can detect a th or caption, but they cannot prove the words are helpful or that every relationship makes sense. Avoid skipping heading levels merely to make a heading look smaller; CSS can change appearance without changing the outline.

title: A consistent product catalog
summary: Design a reusable markup template and check several different content examples.
explanation: Repeated content becomes easier to scan when similar pieces have the same structure. A product card can consistently present a product name, a description, and a price. A reusable markup pattern means you repeat those roles while changing the content. It does not mean every card must have words of the same length. HTML does not automatically calculate prices or create new cards. You author the content, or later write code to produce it, while preserving a meaningful structure for each item.

This complete catalog starts with one card. The same pattern can be copied inside main. ```html Art supplies

Art supplies

Sketch pencils

A set for light and dark lines.

$6

``` article marks a self-contained item that can make sense on its own. h2 names it beneath the catalog's h1. Two p elements contain its description and price.

A class is a reusable name you attach to elements with the class attribute. class="product" identifies all product cards; class="price" identifies price paragraphs. Many elements can share a class. An id instead identifies a single element and should be unique in the document. CSS or a checker can find article.product, meaning an article with the product class. The dot in that selector marks a class; it is not part of the HTML class value. Class names do not create meaning by themselves, so retain real article, heading, and paragraph elements.

Consistency means matching jobs and order. In each card, start with a descriptive h2, follow with a detail paragraph, then a price paragraph bearing class="price". Keep each card's information inside its own article. If the price accidentally sits after </article>, it no longer belongs to the card's structure. Closing tags and indentation make these mistakes easier to see. Do not use h1 for every product simply to make its title larger; h2 shows that these items belong beneath the catalog's overall topic.

Add these cards after the first article, still inside main. ```html

Brush

A small brush for watercolor.

$4

Large mixed-media sketchbook

Thick pages for pencil, ink, and light paint washes.

$18

``` The short and long titles use the same tags. Each article has its own two paragraphs and price class. The dollar sign is visible text here; it does not make the browser interpret a payment or change a number.

A markup template should work with different content. Try a short title, a long title, a brief description, and a longer description. Check that every item keeps a heading, detail, and price. HTML establishes the structure; later CSS determines whether long content wraps and fits. Do not shorten an important name just to hide a layout problem. If you copy a card, update all its content together so its name, description, and price still describe the same item. Repetition helps maintenance only when the repeated pattern stays accurate.

For the garden catalog, create at least three article elements with class="product". Give each a nonempty h2, a detail p, and a p with class="price". The checks look inside each article, so scattered headings and prices elsewhere cannot substitute for complete cards. Then practice adding a fourth card using the same pattern. Review short and long content and explain why the repeated structure helps people scan products. Passing a card-count check does not tell you whether the prices are correct or whether long text fits a future visual design.

title: Style your hobby page
summary: In the starter, find the TODO rule for the heading and set a dark text color.
explanation: CSS means Cascading Style Sheets. It tells the browser how HTML should look: colors, fonts, space, and layout. A selector chooses elements to style. A declaration gives one setting: a property followed by a colon, then a value and a semicolon. In color: navy;, color is the property and navy is its value. Braces { and } contain the declarations that belong to a selector. CSS changes presentation; the HTML still decides whether content is a heading, paragraph, link, or button.

Three common selectors choose elements differently. button selects every button element. .action selects elements with class="action". #start selects the element with id="start". The dot means class, and the hash means id; neither character belongs in the HTML attribute value. A class can be shared. An id should be unique on a page. In this exercise, use the element selector button when the goal is to style all buttons. A class named button is not automatically the same as a button tag.

Readability needs a useful difference between text and background colors. color controls text; background controls the background. A hex color starts with # and uses digits and letters to describe red, green, and blue amounts. A color name such as navy is also a valid value. Two different color codes can still be hard to distinguish, so “different” is not a full contrast test. font-family supplies a list of preferred fonts. If Verdana is unavailable, sans-serif asks for a suitable font without small strokes at the ends of letters.

This complete HTML document shows how a style element can hold CSS for a small page. ```html Reading corner

Reading corner

Choose a book for today.

``` The style content is CSS rather than visible text. The HTML creates the elements the selectors match. This button has a name; additional behavior would be needed to make it browse books.

The box model describes an element's content area, padding, border, and margin. Padding is space inside its border, around its content. Margin is space outside its border, between it and nearby elements. px means CSS pixels, a browser length unit, rather than necessarily one hardware screen dot. Larger positive lengths request more space. padding: 8px 14px uses 8px at top and bottom and 14px at left and right. margin: 18px 0 10px means top 18px, left and right zero, bottom 10px. You can write individual properties when the shorthand order feels confusing.

For the hobby page, give the body a light background, dark text, and a readable font family. Add a dark heading color, a positive top margin for h1, and positive left padding for button. Keep space visible around nearby elements. The checks read the computed style, which is the final style the browser has worked out after matching rules. They verify basic spacing and different colors, but do not prove good contrast or comfortable reading. Change a spacing value and predict which area grows before inspecting it.

analogy.connection: A selector picks which page items get the chosen color and spacing.
analogy.limit: CSS rules describe appearance; they do not change the words or meaning of the page.

title: A profile card that fits
summary: Use a card with `width: 100%` and a `max-width` so it stops growing.
explanation: A responsive card fits the space available instead of assuming every screen is wide. Responsive means adapting to different sizes. A width sets the requested width; max-width caps how large it can become. width: 100% asks for the available width of its containing block, usually its parent here. max-width: 360px stops the card growing beyond 360 CSS pixels. Together they can produce a narrow card on a small screen and a capped card on a large screen. The content, padding, and border still need to fit that width.

With the default content-box sizing, a declared width measures only the content. Padding and borders add extra width outside that measurement. A 300px content width with 12px padding on each side and 2px borders uses 328px in total. border-box includes padding and border in the declared width, so that same declared 300px includes them. Margin remains outside the box in either case. width: 100% plus border-box is useful here because padding will not make the card wider than its parent's available width. Long unbroken content can still overflow, so test the actual content too.

A percentage is a share of a reference size. In this card example, width percentages refer to the containing block's width. 75% of 400px is 0.75 × 400px, or 300px. 60% of 500px is 300px. 100% is the whole available share. A cap can reduce the final size: 100% of a 600px parent asks for 600px, but max-width: 360px stops at 360px. These values describe the CSS box; box-sizing determines whether its padding and border are included. The parent's padding may also affect the available width.

This HTML fragment belongs inside body and works with the previous CSS. Supply a real painter.jpg image file. ```html

A badge often needs a small box that can sit beside text. display: inline-block lets it remain in an inline flow while accepting padding and box dimensions. border-radius rounds its corners; it does not change its meaning. Test the card with a longer description, a large image, and a narrower preview. Horizontal overflow means content sticks past the available width and may cause sideways scrolling. title: An adaptable toolbar
summary: Turn `.toolbar` into a flex container.
explanation: Flexbox is a CSS layout system for arranging items mainly along one direction, such as a row of buttons. The element with display: flex is the flex container. Its direct children become flex items. If a nav contains three buttons, styling the nav as flex arranges those buttons. You do not need to make every button a flex container. A row is the default main direction, and source order means the order of elements in the HTML. Keeping that order helps visual reading and keyboard navigation agree.

Put this HTML fragment inside body. It provides the direct children for the CSS example on the next page.

```html
<nav class="toolbar" aria-label="Drawing tools">
  <button type="button">Pencil</button>
  <button type="button">Brush</button>
  <button type="button">Eraser</button>
</nav>
```

nav describes the group's navigation-like purpose; for a real drawing application, choose semantics that fit the actions and supply their behavior. Each native button has visible words and keyboard behavior. The class attribute lets .toolbar select the group. The HTML order is Pencil, Brush, Eraser, so that is the order to preserve as space changes.

A flex container normally tries to keep items on one line. flex-wrap: wrap allows another line when the current row cannot comfortably contain the items. gap adds space between items and, when wrapped, between lines. It does not add outer padding around the container. justify-content distributes items along the main direction. flex-start places them at the start. justify-content: center changes alignment, but does not enable wrapping. flex-direction: row-reverse changes the visual direction, which can make the displayed order disagree with the original source order.

A media query is a condition around CSS rules. max-width: 460px includes widths equal to 460px as well as smaller ones. min-width would include that width and larger ones. The browser reevaluates the condition when the viewport changes. Because the later .toolbar rule uses the same selector, its gap replaces the earlier gap when the query matches. This is part of the cascade: the browser combines matching declarations to choose the final style. A query's threshold should suit the content; it does not have to be a particular phone model's width.

Space is shared by the items and their gaps. Two items each asking for 50% of a 300px row request 150px + 150px, already filling 300px before any gap. A positive gap needs more room, and other flex sizing rules may change the final item sizes. 25% of 300px is 75px because one quarter means divide by four. Percent math helps you predict requested sizes, but do not assume the final layout ignores padding, borders, gap, or shrinking. The exercise's buttons mainly use their natural content size.

For this toolbar, style .toolbar as flex, enable wrap, and add a gap. Use a media query to reduce that spacing on narrower screens. Keep the supplied buttons in Home, Projects, About source order. The checks inspect flex display, wrap behavior, and that exact HTML order. Then narrow the preview until the buttons wrap, and check that each stays readable and reachable. Do not reorder the buttons just to make one screenshot look neat; the project asks for the same intended sequence at every width.

analogy.connection: Flex items line up in a row and wrap onto another line when needed.
analogy.limit: Flexbox changes visual placement; it should not be used to create a reading order that disagrees with the HTML.

title: A photo gallery
summary: Give `.gallery` a grid display with three equal columns.
explanation: CSS Grid arranges content in rows and columns. The element with display: grid is the grid container; its direct children become grid items. A track is one row or column's space. grid-template-columns defines the columns. repeat(3, 1fr) means make three columns, each with one equal fraction of the remaining space. The browser places ordinary items across those columns in source order and starts new rows as needed. Grid is useful when both horizontal and vertical alignment matter, such as a photo gallery.

gap reserves space between tracks. Subtract the gaps before dividing the remaining width into equal fr shares. A 636px container with four columns and three 12px gaps leaves 600px for tracks, so each track gets 150px. If a question already gives 600px of track space and asks for three equal columns, divide 600 by three to get 200px. Track space and total container width are different when gaps exist. The fr unit is a share of available space, not a fixed number of pixels.

Grid lines mark track boundaries. For columns, lines are numbered starting at the first edge. grid-column: 2 places an item starting at column line 2, which begins the second column in this simple left-to-right grid. It does not mean row 2 or “two columns wide.” grid-column: 2 / 4 starts at line 2 and ends at line 4, spanning two tracks. grid-column: span 2 asks to span two columns without naming a starting line. A slash separates start and end in this property. The quiz uses the simpler single start value.

``` Each img is a direct grid item. class="gallery" selects the container. aria-label names the gallery region when applicable to its semantics, and each informative picture has its own alt description. Images need no closing img tag. Adding another image adds another item; the grid can create another row automatically.

A responsive layout changes when available space changes. The @media query here tests the viewport's width, not an individual image's width. Because it comes after the initial grid rule, its matching column declaration replaces the earlier one. Test just above, exactly at, and just below a threshold to understand max-width's inclusive limit. display: block avoids image baseline spacing, and height: auto avoids stretching the picture into a wrong shape. A narrow grid still needs sensible child content; long unbreakable content can require further sizing rules in other projects.

analogy.limit: A grid cell is a layout area, not a guarantee that an image’s own content will be cropped or scaled.

title: A responsive component set
summary: Define reusable spacing and text-size custom properties on `:root`.
explanation: A component is a reusable piece of an interface, such as a panel with a title and a description. Shared CSS values help several components stay consistent. A custom property is a named value whose name begins with two hyphens, such as --space. Define it on :root, which selects the document's root element, so descendants can normally inherit it. Use var(--space) to read that value. Changing the shared definition then changes the places using it, rather than making you hunt through many repeated numbers.

rem is a length based on the root element's font size. If that font size is 16px, 1.25rem is 20px, though users and styles can change the root size. vw means one percent of the viewport's width; 4vw is 20px in a 500px-wide viewport. font-size sets how large text is. Using relative units can support adaptation, but still test zoom and readability. var() is CSS syntax for reading a custom property; it is not a Swift or JavaScript function. Its parentheses enclose the value name you want.

clamp(minimum, preferred, maximum) chooses a preferred value while keeping it inside the given bounds when the minimum is below the maximum. clamp(12px, 4vw, 24px) gives 12px if the preferred part works out to 8px, 20px if it works out to 20px, and 24px if it works out to 30px. The commas separate its three arguments, meaning the three supplied values. These bounds apply to the resulting CSS length; they do not guarantee that a long heading never wraps or that every person finds the text comfortable.

A media query can test the viewport. A container query can test a qualifying ancestor container. That distinction helps a panel fit in a narrow sidebar inside a wide window. container-type: inline-size enables size queries along the inline direction, usually width in horizontal English text. The query changes descendants of the container; it does not query and restyle the container itself based on its own size. Give the wrapper a real available width through its surrounding layout. title: A progress animation
summary: Define a `fill` keyframe animation from zero width to full width.
explanation: An animation changes a style over time. CSS keyframes define the starting, ending, and possibly middle values. animation applies those keyframes to an element. A progress display also needs understandable information when the motion is absent. Keep a visible text label with the final result, rather than expecting someone to judge a bar's width. This exercise animates an already-complete result for presentation; CSS by itself does not know whether an actual upload has completed. A real progress display would receive its value from the work being done.

The animation name must match the @keyframes name exactly. A duration gives how long one run takes. A timing function describes how the visual change moves through that run. linear moves evenly; ease-out slows near the end. both is a fill mode: it applies the starting frame during any delay and keeps the ending frame after completion. It does not cause repeated playback. No repeat count is given here, so the normal run happens once. A final base width of 100% also preserves the full bar if animation is disabled.

Some people prefer less motion because moving content can be distracting or uncomfortable. Their device or browser can expose a reduced-motion preference. Use @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) to respond to that choice. This media feature is not a keyframe name or an animation delay value. Disabling this animation should still show the complete result, rather than leaving an empty bar. Do not make people wait for a moving graphic to obtain important information that could be available immediately in text.

A fraction tells how much of a total has passed. If two seconds have passed in a four-second run, 2 ÷ 4 is 0.5, or 50% of its time. With linear movement from zero width to full width, that also gives half the width. With ease-out, half the time does not necessarily give half the width: the timing function changes the relationship. The exercise uses ease-out, while its math question asks about a linear animation's time fraction. Keep elapsed time and displayed progress distinct whenever the movement is not linear.

For the project, define @keyframes fill from width: 0 to width: 100%, then apply fill to .bar. Keep the supplied 100% label. Add the reduced-motion media query, set animation: none there, and leave width: 100%. The checks choose the expected animation name based on the current preference and look for the query and label. Try both preference states using an appropriate browser testing control, and inspect the end state after motion finishes. A bar's width cannot establish actual upload success; it illustrates the supplied final state.

analogy.connection: Keyframes define the fill journey; a reduced-motion preference can skip the journey and show its endpoint.
analogy.limit: A CSS animation does not measure real task completion; this demo’s percentage is a supplied value.

These empty elements draw shapes when styled, but they do not explain the diagram's meaning. A real informative diagram also needs readable labels or a text description that explains what the shapes represent.

top: 50% places a child's top edge halfway down the reference area's height. left: 50% places its left edge halfway across the reference area's width. The reference here is the diagram's inner padding box, which excludes its border. In the standalone example, box-sizing: content-box explicitly gives that area a width of 320px and height of 180px, without padding, so the starting coordinates are 160px from its left and 90px from its top. A transform changes how an element is drawn. rotate(45deg) turns it by an angle. deg means degrees: a full turn is 360 degrees, a half turn is 180 degrees, and a quarter turn is 90 degrees. translateX(6px) shifts along an x direction; scale() would resize the drawing. A rotated pointer can therefore reach outside its original rectangle, so inspect its actual position and edges.

transform-origin chooses the pivot for rotation and scaling. 0 50% means the left edge and halfway down the element's own height. That gives a pointer a pivot near its starting end instead of its center. Transform order matters: rotate(45deg) translateX(6px) composes a translation followed by rotation, so the translation is rotated too and the pointer shifts along its turned direction. Reversing those function names changes the result. The percentages in transform-origin refer to the transformed element's box, while top and left percentages here use the containing reference area.

title: A temperature checker
summary: Keep the supplied temperature at 24 and comfort limit at 22.
explanation: A type is the kind of value you have. JavaScript uses numbers for calculations, strings for text, and Booleans for yes-or-no results. `17` is a number; `"17"` is a string containing two characters. `true` and `false` have no quotes because they are Boolean values. A comparison checks how two values relate and produces one of these Booleans.

The signs `<` and `>` mean less than and greater than. The signs `<=` and `>=` include equality too: less than or equal to, and greater than or equal to. `===` is strict equality, which compares without changing the values' types. A single `=` assigns a value. Use assignment to store the answer from a comparison, such as `const below = temperature < limit;`.

Strict equality also checks the type. `"19" === 19` is false because text and a number are different kinds of values. `19 === 19` is true. Automatically changing one type into another is called coercion. JavaScript has comparison forms that allow coercion, but `===` avoids it. Keep temperatures and limits numeric here; do not add quotation marks to them just because they will be displayed later.

You can reason about each answer without running code. Put the two numbers on a number line, then ask the question written by the sign. In the exercise, 24 lies to the right of 22: below is false, equality is false, and above is true. `24 >= 22` is also true. With a value of 21 and a limit of 22, below becomes true. These are separate questions, not three steps that alter the temperature.

Check three cases: a value below the limit, exactly at the limit, and above the limit. Each comparison should agree with the case. Printing the named answers in order lets you see which question each result answers. The stored Booleans are actual values, so `above === true` checks that the above comparison produced true. An output string saying "true" and the Boolean `true` are different values even though they may look alike on screen.

analogy.connection: Comparison operators tell the program which side of the mark a number falls on.
analogy.limit: A Boolean reports true or false; it does not explain why the temperature has that value.

explanation: Sometimes the next action depends on a value. A condition is a question that produces true or false. An `if` statement checks a condition and runs its block only when the answer is true. A block is code grouped inside braces `{}`. An `else if` supplies another question when the earlier one was false, and a final `else` handles anything still unmatched.

The setting is a string, so compare it with quoted text using strict equality `===`. Exact spelling matters: `"easy"` and `"Easy"` are different strings. Declare a message with `let` because your branches will assign its selected value afterward. Unlike `const`, `let` allows reassignment. `let message = "";` starts with an empty string, which contains no characters.

An if/else chain selects at most one branch. After one branch runs, JavaScript skips the later branches in that chain. Parentheses after `if` and `else if` contain the condition; braces contain the action. An `else` has no condition because it covers the remaining possibilities. A semicolon ends each assignment, while a closing brace ends its block.

Your project needs three known settings, so give easy, medium, and hard their own comparisons. The expected messages are "Take your time", "Ready for a challenge", and "Expert mode". The final else should assign "Unknown setting". With the supplied medium value, the easy test fails and the medium test succeeds. With hard, the first two tests fail and the third succeeds.

This exercise assigns and prints a message; it does not need `return` because its code is outside a function. If you see a short branch such as `if (condition) message = "text";`, JavaScript allows a single statement without braces. Braces make the grouping easier to see and let you safely add another statement. Try each setting, then an unknown one, and predict which block runs before reading the output.

title: A countdown display
summary: Create an empty `countdown` array.
explanation: A loop repeats a block of instructions. One trip through the block is an iteration. A countdown needs three decisions: where the number starts, when another iteration is allowed, and how the number changes afterward. A `for` loop places these three parts inside parentheses. The code inside braces is called its body.

Read `for (let n = 4; n >= 1; n--)` as: start n at 4; keep going while n is at least 1; decrease n by 1 after each body. The two semicolons inside the header separate these parts. They are part of the loop syntax, not instructions to remove. `n--` is a short way of subtracting one from n. The update happens after the body, before the next condition check.

Trace the stopping point carefully. At n = 1 the condition `n >= 1` is true, so 1 is added. The update makes n = 0. Now the condition is false, and the loop stops. It never adds 0. Four values were added. `.length` is the number of array entries, and square brackets read one entry by its index, which starts at 0. For four entries, the last index is 3.

Every repeat must move toward stopping. If you start above 1 but increase n instead of decreasing it, `n >= 1` can stay true forever. A missing update can cause the same problem. This is called an infinite loop. Write the start, condition, and update together, then mentally follow at least two iterations and the final condition check.

For the required countdown, start at 5 and include 1. The five visited numbers are 5, 4, 3, 2, 1. Store them in `countdown`, then print the joined result. Its length should be 5; indexes 0 and 4 hold 5 and 1. In checks, `&&` means both questions must be true, such as checking the first and last entry together. Counting values and counting array indexes are different: five entries occupy indexes 0 through 4.

analogy.familiar: Calling out numbers as someone walks down five steps.
analogy.connection: The counter moves down one step each time through the loop.
analogy.limit: A loop repeats code; it does not automatically know when a countdown should end.

An index is an entry's position. JavaScript starts indexes at zero: the first entry is at 0, the second at 1, and the third at 2. Reading `tools[0]` gets the first entry. The brackets after a name mean read at this position; brackets in a declaration create the array. `.length` gives the count of entries, which is not the last index.

`.push()` is an array method: a function belonging to an array. Call it with the new item inside parentheses. It changes the existing array by adding at the end. The word mutable means changeable. An array is mutable. A `const` declaration prevents assigning a completely different array to that name, but it does not prevent adding or updating entries in the current array.

An empty array has length 0 and no final entry. With an ordinary nonempty list, last index equals length minus one. Asking for an index that has no entry produces `undefined` rather than a real packed item. Be careful with `list[list.length]`: for a three-entry array it asks for index 3, which is one past the final existing entry.

title: A reusable distance converter
summary: Write `convertDistance(distance, factor)`.
explanation: A function packages steps so you can use them again with different inputs. Defining a function describes the steps; calling it runs them. The definition begins with `function`, followed by its name, parentheses for input names, and braces around the body. A converter multiplies the distance by a conversion factor, a number that tells you how much to scale it.

A parameter is a name for an input inside the function. An argument is the actual value supplied by the calling code. In `function scale(value, factor)`, value and factor are parameters. In `scale(4, 3)`, 4 and 3 are arguments. Commas separate inputs. Their order matters: the first argument fills the first parameter and the second fills the second.

Returning and displaying are separate actions. `return 6;` makes the caller receive 6; it does not put 6 on screen. `console.log(6);` displays 6; it does not make a function return 6. A function with no return value returns `undefined`. Keep the converter's calculation in its return so other code and the checks can use the result, even without displaying it.

The project function is named `convertDistance` and needs the two supplied parameters. Return their product. The checks call your function directly with zero and with several other distances and factors. For 3 and 2, the product is 6; for 5 and 1.6, it is 8. Using the parameters rather than returning a fixed number makes all these calls work.

A conversion factor includes a meaning, such as destination units per original unit. Keep that direction in mind: multiplication uses the factor supplied for this lesson. Multiplying by the factor converts the distance but does not edit an outside variable that held the original number. You can inspect a returned value by placing the call inside `console.log(...)`; the inner call finishes first, then its result becomes the argument of the display function.

analogy.connection: The function receives a value and factor, multiplies them, then returns the answer.
analogy.limit: Returning a result does not print it; display is a separate action.

Write braces `{}` around an object, a colon `:` between each property name and value, and commas between properties. One character object can hold text for its name, a number for its health, and an array for its equipment.

Dot notation reads a named property. `character.health` means get the health property of character. Add `= 9` to replace that property's value. This assignment targets one property; it does not replace the whole object. To read an item inside an array property, combine dot notation with an index, such as `character.equipment[0]`.

Declaring the variable with `const` keeps the name attached to this object; it does not freeze the properties. `character.health = 9;` is allowed. Property spelling matters just like variable spelling. `health` and `Health` refer to different properties. Reading an absent property normally gives `undefined`. title: A flexible greeting tool
summary: Write two functions that return different greetings for a name.
explanation: A function is also a value in JavaScript. You can give it a name, pass it as an argument, and let another function call it. A function received this way is called a callback. A higher-order function is one that receives or returns a function. These names describe what the code does; there is no extra magic syntax needed to pass a callback.

Distinguish the function from its result. `friendly` means the function itself. `friendly("Noor")` calls it immediately and means the value it returns. If a receiving function expects something it can call, pass the function name without parentheses. Its parameter can then hold that function value and call it with an input.

Backticks make a template literal, a string that can insert values. Inside it, `${name}` evaluates name and adds its value to the text. The dollar sign and braces mark the insertion; ordinary quoted strings do not perform this insertion. Function parentheses contain inputs, function braces contain instructions, and template-literal braces surround an expression to insert. Their meaning comes from where they appear.

The exercise also puts returned greetings on a page. In a browser, `document` represents the page. `document.querySelector("#g1")` finds the element with id g1; the `#` marks an id in this selector string. Assigning its `.textContent` sets its plain text. That requires the supplied HTML elements to exist. It does not treat the greeting as HTML instructions, so angle brackets in text stay text.

Your two supplied callbacks are friendly and playful. Pass each to showGreeting with Ari to obtain the expected two different messages. Store each result, then assign it to the matching page element's textContent. These callbacks run when showGreeting calls them; a callback can also be saved and called later in other designs. The browser elements are practice fixtures, while the main skill is passing a function and using its returned value.

title: A cleaner score report
summary: Use the supplied player object with name and score.
explanation: You can make a readable sentence from information stored in an object. An object groups named properties, such as a player's name and score. Destructuring is a short way to read several properties into variables at once. It saves repeated property reads; it does not convert numbers into text or create a live connection to later changes.

Read `const { name, score } = player;` as: read player.name into name, and player.score into score. The property names inside the braces must match the source object. Here the braces are a destructuring pattern, not a new object. `const` means each extracted variable cannot be reassigned. For numeric and string properties, you receive their current values.

Template literals use backticks rather than ordinary quotation marks. `${...}` marks a place where JavaScript evaluates an expression and includes its result in the string. The dollar sign starts the insertion and the braces contain the expression. Text outside the braces stays as written, including spaces and punctuation. Numbers are represented as text in the resulting sentence without changing the original number variable.

Keep names precise. A missing property yields undefined, so a misspelled destructuring name can put undefined into a report. A single equals sign assigns the extracted values; `===` compares values. Destructuring an object property that is itself an object shares that object's reference, but the exercise extracts only a string and a number. For those values, later replacing player.score does not update the extracted score variable.

Your supplied player is Kai with 18 points. Extract name and score, then use both in the expected sentence and preserve its period. The check also confirms score remains the number 18. For the math example, the expression 4 + 2 inside `${}` evaluates to 6 before the surrounding text becomes `Score: 6`. First identify the inserted expressions, evaluate them, and only then read the finished sentence.

title: A workout summary
summary: Use the supplied minutes `[20, 35, 45]` and keep sessions of 30 minutes or more.
explanation: Processing a list often takes three steps: select some entries, transform the selected entries, and combine their values. An array method is a function attached to an array. `filter` selects, `map` transforms, and `reduce` combines. Each receives a callback, a function it calls for individual entries. This project selects long sessions, converts their minutes to seconds, and calculates a total and average.

An arrow function is another way to write a function. `m => m >= 30` means take an input called m and return the comparison. With two inputs, use parentheses: `(sum, x) => sum + x`. The arrow `=>` introduces the function body; it is different from `>=`, which compares numbers. For a short expression body, the arrow function returns that expression automatically.

Reduce carries an accumulated answer from one entry to the next. `seconds.reduce((sum, x) => sum + x, 0)` starts sum at 0, then adds each x. title: A reaction timer
summary: Record a start timestamp when the signal is shown.
explanation: A timestamp records when something happened. JavaScript's `Date.now()` gives a timestamp measured in milliseconds since a fixed reference date. A millisecond is one thousandth of a second. To measure a duration, subtract the earlier timestamp from the later one. The result is elapsed time, not a clock reading. Both numbers must use the same unit and reference.

The program needs state: stored information that can change between actions. Use let for the saved start and elapsed values. `null` means there is no recorded value yet. Use null rather than 0 as the missing marker because zero can be a valid timestamp or duration. A signal saves a starting time; a later click can calculate the difference.

`!==` means strict inequality: are these values different? The guard allows calculation only when startedAt is different from null. An early click must be ignored because no signal time exists. `Math.max(a, b)` chooses the larger number. Taking the maximum of 0 and the difference prevents a negative duration when supplied times are out of order. It cannot turn a bad clock reading into a reliable measurement.

In a real browser button, a click event listener can call `clickAt(Date.now())` when clicked. The signal action would call `signal(Date.now())` at its starting moment. Pass a function to addEventListener so the browser can run it later. Your exercise tests the timing functions with fixed numbers instead, which makes the expected difference predictable and repeatable without waiting for a person's click.

The supplied round begins at 1000 and clicks at 1240, so elapsed is 240 milliseconds. For 500 and 650, it is 150 milliseconds. Check normal, early, and reset cases separately. Starting a new signal should clear the previous elapsed result; reset should clear the start too. A timing measurement from this simple clock is a practice estimate, and real applications may use a monotonic clock for durations that must ignore wall-clock adjustments.

analogy.connection: Store the first timestamp; subtract it from the click timestamp.
analogy.limit: This small demo uses wall-clock time; production timing may use a monotonic clock to avoid system clock adjustments.

title: A data-loading card
summary: Create `loadCard(fetchData)` as an async function.
explanation: Some work finishes later, such as obtaining data. A Promise represents an eventual result. It can be pending while unfinished, fulfilled with a value, or rejected with a reason. A rejection means that operation failed. A Promise is not the data itself, so code must wait for the result before using it as loaded data.

An `async` function always returns a Promise. Inside it, `await` pauses that function until a Promise settles. It lets other work proceed while waiting; it does not freeze the whole browser. If the Promise fulfills, await produces its value. If it rejects, await throws the rejection so a surrounding catch block can handle it.

The try block contains work that can fail. A catch block receives the thrown error when that happens; error.message is its explanatory text. `new Error("Offline")` creates an error object. The function parameter getData is a callback: the loader calls it to start the supplied work. `Promise.resolve(value)` creates a fulfilled Promise; `Promise.reject(error)` creates a rejected one.

Represent each stage explicitly: idle before loading, loading while waiting, success with data, and error with a message. This gives a page enough information to show the right card. Object shorthand `{ status: "success", data }` means the data property holds the variable data. This exercise stores these states in an object; displaying a real card would read that object and update page elements.

In your project, showSuccess and showError create the final states, and loadCard sets loading before calling and awaiting fetchData. Store the returned Promise as successfulLoad. `instanceof Promise` checks whether an object is a Promise; it does not prove success or verify the final displayed data. The checks exercise the state helpers too. Use an awaited demo to inspect a completed load; reading state immediately after starting a load can still see loading.

analogy.connection: The Promise settles later, and the card switches from loading to success or error.
analogy.limit: This lesson uses supplied Promise scenarios; a real network request can fail, take longer, or return invalid data.

title: A reusable game character
summary: Create a `Character` class with a name and health.
explanation: A class describes how to create objects with related fields and actions. An object created from a class is an instance. Each character instance needs its own name and health. A method is a function defined on the class that instances can use. This lets you reuse the damage calculation while keeping each character's changing health separate.

`class Character` starts a class definition. Its braces contain methods. The constructor is the method run when `new Character(...)` creates an instance. Its parameters receive the supplied values. `this` refers to the instance whose method is running. Assigning `this.health = health` puts the input number into that particular object's health property.

Damage subtracts from the current health. `Math.max(0, difference)` chooses whichever is larger, ensuring health does not fall below zero. This lower bound is inclusive, so zero is permitted. Without the maximum, taking 20 damage from 14 health would produce -6. This rule applies to nonnegative damage amounts as supplied; negative damage would increase health, so a larger application would define and validate its allowed inputs.

The method changes a property and does not return the updated health. Inspect `.health` after calling it. This differs from a pure converter function that returns a new number without editing an object. `const fern` is allowed because the name stays attached to the instance even while its properties change. Constructor and method definitions inside a class omit the function keyword.

Your instances are Luna at 10 and Sol at 8. Damage 3 leaves Luna at 7 while Sol stays at 8. A later large damage amount must leave Luna at zero. For the quiz, 8 minus 3 leaves 5. Test ordinary subtraction, unchanged second-instance state, and the zero boundary; together these show that methods operate on the right object and obey the chosen health limit.

title: A route search game
summary: Use the supplied graph with start A and target F.
explanation: A graph describes places and their connections. A node is one place; an edge is one connection. An adjacency list records each node's neighbors, such as `{ P: ["Q", "R"] }`. A path lists nodes traveled through. Four nodes along one path have three edges because an edge joins each consecutive pair. This lesson searches for a path to a target node.

Breadth-first search, or BFS, visits nearby nodes before farther ones. Its queue stores discovered nodes waiting to be processed. A queue takes the oldest added entry first: push adds at the end of an array and shift removes its first entry. Each queue entry can hold the node and its path. A Set records seen nodes; it keeps each name only once and supports has and add.

`while (queue.length)` repeats while the queue has entries. Destructuring `[node, path]` reads the two parts removed by shift. `visited++` increases the count by one. `graph[node]` reads neighbors using a variable as a property key. `|| []` supplies an empty array if the lookup is missing. The for/of loop visits each neighbor. `!seen.has(next)` means the node has not already been seen. The spread `...path` copies the path's entries into a new array before adding next.

In an unweighted graph, every edge counts equally, so BFS finds a path with the fewest edges. When two paths tie, neighbor order decides which is discovered first. Seen nodes prevent endless revisits around cycles, where connections lead back to earlier places. Marking a node when adding it to the queue avoids adding it repeatedly. If the queue empties without reaching the target, return null for the path and the measured visit count.

The exercise graph's BFS tie is resolved by its neighbor order, producing A-B-D-F: four nodes, three edges. All six reachable nodes may be visited before F is processed. A missing target Z returns path null. Compare approaches on the same graph and state what you counted; a visit count on one graph does not prove one search is always faster. Array shift and path copies also cost work, so visits are a useful measure here rather than a complete benchmark.

analogy.familiar: Finding rooms using a map: check all nearby rooms before going farther, or follow one hallway until it ends.
analogy.connection: BFS explores by distance layers; DFS explores one path deeply.
analogy.limit: A measured visit count depends on the graph and neighbor order; it is not a general runtime benchmark.

title: A responsive search tool
summary: Increase `latestId` each time a search starts.
explanation: A search can start before an earlier search finishes. Responses may arrive in the opposite order from their requests. If an old response is displayed just because it arrived last, it can replace the answer the user currently wants. A request id is a number assigned when a request starts; keep the largest, newest id so the program can identify current work.

Use let for the newest id and the visible text because they change. Start the id at zero, then use `latestId++` to add one for each search. A Set holds canceled ids without duplicates. `.add(id)` records one, and `.has(id)` checks membership. Marking an old id canceled is bookkeeping in this fixture; it does not stop a real network operation.

The guard contains two questions joined by `&&`, meaning both must be true. The strict equality asks whether the result belongs to the newest id. The exclamation mark `!` means not, so `!cancelledIds.has(id)` asks whether it has not been canceled. The function only assigns visibleResult inside this guard. A stale result leaves the current text alone.

For real browser fetch work, an AbortController can request cancellation. Create a controller, pass its `.signal` in fetch's options, and call `.abort()` when the work becomes outdated. The request can reject with an abort error. Cancellation may arrive after completion, and stopping the client does not prove the server did no work. Keep the id guard as well. The supplied exercise models cancellation using a set rather than making actual fetch calls.

In your exercise, oldId must be smaller than newId. Mark oldId canceled when starting the new request, display "new answer", and ignore "old answer" even when it arrives afterward. Arrival time does not change which request is current. Tests should vary response order and confirm that stale text never overwrites current text. The canceled-id set grows in this small fixture; a long-running application could remove entries once the old work can no longer return.

analogy.connection: A request number marks which result is current.
analogy.limit: Cancellation is a request to stop work, not proof that every operation stopped; stale-result checks still matter.
