title: Model separate inventories
summary: Use a class so two game inventories each keep their own items and quantities.
explanation: A class describes a kind of object with stored information and functions that use it. An instance is one actual object created from that class. If Inventory is the class, Inventory() constructs a new inventory instance. Calling it twice creates two independent objects. A property stores information belonging to an instance, and a method performs a job on that instance. Each inventory should keep its own quantities so adding a potion to one bag does not silently put it in another bag.

A dictionary pairs keys with values. [String: Int] means String keys and Int values. Here a key is an item name, and its value is the quantity. [:] is an empty dictionary; [] would be an empty array. quantities[stamp, default: 0] uses the quantity for that key, or zero if none exists. When used with += amount, it stores the increased quantity back under that key. This prevents a missing item from becoming an unsafe missing-value calculation. Dictionary keys are unique; adding the same name updates its quantity rather than creating a second identical key.

private(set) lets outside code read quantities but restricts setting it directly to the permitted scope, so the class can control updates through methods. func add has an unlabeled item argument and an amount parameter with default 1. album.add("flower") therefore adds one. guard amount > 0 else { return } exits early when the amount is not positive. guard checks a condition that must be true before the remaining code continues. The plus-equals operator increases a stored value: quantity += amount has the same numeric effect as assigning quantity + amount back.

Validation protects quantities from updates you do not allow. In the inventory exercise, positive additions are accepted; zero and negative additions are ignored. Starting at zero and accepting only positive additions keeps quantities nonnegative. It does not impose a maximum automatically. If a different game says quantities must stay from 0 through 5, six is invalid because it is above five; you would need an additional check for that game's limit. Test the boundary and the values just outside it. A stated range and the implemented guard must agree.

For this project, define Inventory with its private-set dictionary, add method, and quantity(of:) method. Construct first and second independently with Inventory(). Add two potions to first and one key to second; second should report zero potions. Ignore amounts zero and below. Checks call the methods and also try nonpositive additions. Explain why second = first would share an object, while second = Inventory() would create another. Keep the method labels and defaults so both add("key") and add("potion", amount: 2) work as intended.

analogy.familiar: Two players’ backpacks
analogy.connection: Each inventory object is like one player’s backpack, with its own contents.
analogy.limit: A class instance is shared when you pass the reference around, so changes can be seen by other owners of that same instance.

steps: Define an Inventory class with a private-set item dictionary.
Add a method that increases one item quantity.
Create first and second independently. Add 2 potions to first and 1 key to second; second must still have 0 potions.

checks.label: Non-positive additions are ignored
checks.expression: { let trial = Inventory(); trial.add("key", amount: 0); trial.add("key", amount: -1); return trial.quantity(of: "key") == 0 }()

quiz.question: Which statement about two `Inventory()` calls is true?
choices: They share one stored dictionary automatically
quiz.explanation: Each initializer call creates a distinct object with its own stored properties.

hints: Store counts in a dictionary keyed by item name.
Use dictionary defaulting so a new item starts at zero.
Only change `self`’s quantities in `add`, then compare the two objects.

math.explanation: Bounds and quantities that must remain consistent: Write the valid range or conserved quantity and check boundary cases.
math.question: A quantity must stay between 0 and 5. Is 6 valid?
choices: No, it is above the maximum
No, because it is not zero
math.feedback: The stated maximum is 5, so 6 is outside the allowed range.

title: Plan trips with flexible details
summary: Represent missing details safely and let several transport types provide their own descriptions.
explanation: Some information can be missing. An optional type explicitly allows either a value or no value. String? means an optional String; nil means it currently has no String. nil is not the empty String "": an empty String exists but contains no characters. Do not assume an optional always has a value. The nil-coalescing operator ?? chooses a fallback when the optional is nil. That makes a missing trip note explainable instead of forcing a value and risking a crash.

This complete program safely displays optional notes.

```swift
struct Visit {
    var destination: String
    var note: String?
}
let firstVisit = Visit(destination: "Astoria", note: nil)
let secondVisit = Visit(destination: "Bend", note: "Bring a jacket")
let firstNote = firstVisit.note ?? "No extra note"
let secondNote = secondVisit.note ?? "No extra note"
print(firstNote)
print(secondNote)
```

The output is No extra note and Bring a jacket. struct defines a value type with named properties. Swift supplies an initializer using those stored property names. The question mark marks the optional type; the doubled question marks are a different operator that supplies the default.

A protocol describes requirements that different types agree to provide. It lets a function use the shared ability without knowing the exact type. A Transport protocol can require a String description, and Train and Bicycle can each provide their own. Conforming means declaring that a type meets the protocol and implementing the requirements. In var description: String { get }, get requires that callers can read the property; it does not require storage or prevent a conforming type from also permitting changes. A computed property calculates or returns its value when read.

Structs have value semantics: assigning a struct to another variable gives a value that can be changed independently. With a Visit value, var copy = original followed by copy.destination = "Another place" does not replace original.destination. Classes instead use references to objects, as you saw with inventory. That difference helps you plan what should change together. A protocol does not by itself make every conforming value a struct or give it value semantics; the concrete type matters. Here the trip and transport models use structs, so their own stored values follow struct behavior.

To read an optional without a fallback, if let can unwrap it safely: if let note = trip.note { ... } runs its block only when a String exists. A force unwrap, written trip.note!, assumes a value and fails at runtime if nil is present. Do not use it for these possibly missing notes. Input ranges need similar deliberate handling: if a valid trip length is 1 through 30 days, zero is below the minimum and 31 is above the maximum. The model in this exercise stores destination and note, not days, so it does not automatically enforce that separate practice range.

For the planner, define Transport with a readable description, conforming Train and Bicycle structs, and Trip with destination and optional note. tripSummary should use any Transport and fall back to No extra note when note is nil. Use Salem with Train and nil for summary; use Eugene with Bicycle and Pack a light for bikeSummary. The checks need those destination, transport, and note words in the outputs. Build the message through properties and interpolation so changing the transport changes its text. Explain the nil case and a present note before building the summary.

analogy.familiar: A form with optional boxes
analogy.connection: An optional is like a form field that may be left blank, and a protocol is like a shared instruction each transport follows.
analogy.limit: A blank optional still needs a useful explanation; silently replacing every missing value can hide important information.

steps: Define a Transport protocol with a description property.
Add two conforming transport structs and a Trip with optional notes.
Use Salem with nil notes and Train for summary; use Eugene with "Pack a light" and Bicycle for bikeSummary. Fall back to "No extra note" for nil.

quiz.question: What does `String?` mean?
choices: The value may be a String or nil
The value is always a String
The value is always an integer
quiz.explanation: The question mark marks an optional String that may have no value.

hints: The protocol requires only one shared property.
Use `??` or `if let` to handle an optional note.
Include the destination, transport description, and a safe note in the returned String.

math.explanation: Valid input ranges: State allowed inputs and check missing, boundary, and invalid values.
math.question: A valid trip length must be 1 through 30 days. Is 0 valid?
choices: No, it is below the minimum
Yes, because zero is a number
math.feedback: The valid range starts at 1, so zero is outside it.

title: Make a practice tracker screen
summary: Build a small SwiftUI form and list backed by local state.
explanation: SwiftUI is Apple's system for describing app screens in Swift. A view describes what appears on screen for the current data. When view-owned state changes, SwiftUI refreshes the affected view description. @State marks that local changeable state. A property wrapper is an annotation that gives a property extra storage behavior; the @ introduces it. This screen's draft is the text being entered, and entries is the list of accepted text. Those are different pieces of state, so adding an entry can update the list and clear the draft independently.

Text draws words. TextField provides editable text. VStack arranges its child views vertically. NavigationStack supplies a navigation container and supports a screen title. Braces in body and the stacks group child-view descriptions; SwiftUI uses result-building behavior to combine those expressions. A modifier is a method that produces a view with a requested change. .padding() adds surrounding space; .textFieldStyle(.roundedBorder) asks for a rounded input style; .navigationTitle("Practice") supplies a title to the navigation system. A leading dot such as .roundedBorder lets Swift infer the type of that named style from context.

A TextField needs a binding, which is a connection that can read and write another piece of state. $draft gives the projected binding for a @State property named draft. Passing plain draft would pass a String value, not the writable connection expected by text:. @Binding is used when a view receives such a connection from another owner; it is not the wrapper that creates this screen's own storage. private keeps the state implementation inside the view's allowed scope. Local @State lasts with the view's state lifetime, but does not automatically persist data across app launches.

trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespacesAndNewlines) removes leading and trailing space and line-break characters. It does not delete spaces inside a sentence. isEmpty asks whether the cleaned String has no characters. ! means NOT, so guard !cleaned.isEmpty permits only nonempty text. observations.indices gives valid array positions, starting at zero. { index in ... } names the current position, and observations[index] reads its text. In id: \.self, the key-path notation tells List to use each index itself as that row's identity. Duplicate text can then make two rows. These index identities suit this append-only example; deleting or reordering items would need a more durable identity design.

For the practice tracker, use local @State for draft and entries, the editable field, Add entry action, and the List inside the navigation container. The supplied screen uses these form controls in VStack; it does not wrap them in a separate Form view. Run in the agreed Apple environment: a browser preview or command-line compiler does not host this iOS screen. Test a nonempty entry, whitespace-only input, and the same text twice. Expect one added row and cleared field for valid input, no row for whitespace-only input, and two rows for duplicate text. A session from 2:15 to 2:45 lasts 30 minutes because the minute difference is 45 - 15 = 30; storing or displaying time would require additional model fields beyond this text-only screen.

analogy.familiar: A whiteboard list
analogy.connection: Local state is like the list on a whiteboard: changing it changes what everyone sees on that screen.
analogy.limit: State in one view is temporary unless you add persistence or share it with another owner.

steps: Create a new iOS App project in Xcode using SwiftUI.
Replace the generated view with the supplied tracker screen.
Run in an iOS Simulator, add a non-empty practice entry, and inspect the list.

quiz.question: Which property wrapper marks view-owned changeable state?
quiz.explanation: @State gives the view a value that can change and trigger a refreshed view.

hints: Bind the text field to `$draft`.
Trim the draft before deciding whether it is empty.
Append valid text to `entries` and clear `draft` so the list refreshes.

math.explanation: Time differences and units: Subtract two timestamps and convert the result into the displayed unit.
math.question: A session begins at 2:15 and ends at 2:45. How long is it?
math.feedback: Subtract 2:15 from 2:45 to get 30 minutes.

externalNotes: SwiftUI screen: create an iOS App project in Xcode, keep the generated @main App entry point, and replace ContentView.swift with solution. Run in an iOS Simulator. Manual rubric: non-empty text adds one row and clears the field; whitespace-only input adds no row; the list updates immediately. SwiftUI checks are manual because the companion compiler does not host an iOS interface. Add the same text twice and verify two rows; the row IDs use stable append-only indexes so duplicate text does not share an identity.

title: Load data with cancellation
summary: Use an actor for shared entries and a cancellable task so older results cannot replace newer ones.
explanation: Asynchronous work can pause while waiting and resume later. async marks a Swift function that may suspend. await marks a call where your code can suspend while that work completes. Suspension lets other work make progress; it does not promise a particular thread or completion order. If one request starts first but takes longer, it may finish after a newer request. A loader therefore needs a deliberate policy: only the still-current request may change the visible result. Merely adding a longer delay cannot establish that policy.

Task represents asynchronous work. Task { ... } starts a task with a closure containing its instructions. A stored Task<Void, Never>? means an optional task whose successful result is Void, no useful returned value, and whose exposed failure type is Never, meaning it does not throw an error out to its caller. The closure can still perform throwing work if it handles the error internally. task?.cancel() uses optional chaining: call cancel only if a task exists. Cancellation is cooperative. It signals that the work should stop; code must check or reach a cancellation-aware operation. Task.checkCancellation() throws if cancellation has been requested, and Task.isCancelled reads that state as a Bool.

Assign every request an increasing number. Increase requestID when starting new work and capture its value in a constant such as thisRequest. A helper accepts(request:current:) should return request == current, a Bool asking whether that request is still the latest one. If request 8 starts, then request 9 starts, only 9 remains current. If 9 finishes first, its result may be displayed; the late 8 result must be ignored. Cancellation alone is not enough because a task could finish before noticing the signal. Check both cancellation and the request ID after every await before updating protected data. In a guard with comma-separated conditions, every condition must succeed. !Task.isCancelled means cancellation has not been requested. += 1 increases the ID by one. In the supplied delay expression, condition ? first : second chooses one of two values, so request 1 gets the slower delay.

An actor protects its stored state through isolation: outside code must use its allowed access paths rather than changing the storage freely. actor PracticeStore can own its entries and accepted request number. Calls across the actor boundary use await because access may require waiting for that actor. Within its replacement method, guard request >= requestID else { return } rejects a response older than the last one stored. >= means greater than or equal to. That comparison accepts a newer replacement or a repeat of the same request. The loader's stricter equality check establishes which request is current; the store's number check separately prevents an old replacement from overwriting newer stored data.

@MainActor isolates the loader's state and methods to the main actor, the executor normally used for UI work. It does not make every operation inside an async method run without interruption. While an await suspends a method, other actor work may run and change its state. That is why a guard before await store.replace is not a substitute for another guard after it. private(set) allows reading a property outside its setting scope while keeping updates controlled. A method cancel should signal the task, increase requestID so old work is stale, and set an understandable message. It should preserve existing useful results unless the design deliberately says otherwise.

Model the loader's states in ordinary words: Ready before a request, Loading during it, Loaded with entries after success, Could not load after failure, or Load cancelled after cancellation. An outdated task should not change either the result or the current message. catch is CancellationError recognizes that error type; a following catch handles other errors. if accepts(...) inside those catches prevents a stale task from replacing a newer message. The supplied driver uses MainActor.run to read or construct main-actor state from its async context. It also stores two values in a tuple, accessed as .0 and .1, to inspect the result and message together.

For the exercise, use the supplied real async driver: slow request 1 followed by faster request 2 should leave session-2 in both the loader and actor store. Request 0 should produce Could not load practice data. Explicit cancellation of request 1 should preserve session-2 and show Load cancelled. Store and cancel the Task, capture each new ID, and guard after awaits; do not depend on delays alone. In the math scenario, request A with ID 4 remains stale once B with ID 5 is current, so B stays visible even if A finishes last. Compile and run with the compatible Mac companion or Apple toolchain, then test in Xcode when attaching a real interface. The browser cannot execute this Swift concurrency or prove its scheduling behavior.

analogy.familiar: A deli ticket
analogy.connection: A request ID works like a ticket number: only the currently served ticket may update the display.
analogy.limit: Cancellation does not instantly erase work; the operation must reach a cancellation check or support cancellation itself.

steps: Make accepts true only for the current request ID, and let PracticeStore reject older replacement IDs.
In Loader.start, cancel the previous task, capture a new request ID, and check cancellation plus that ID after each await.
Use the supplied scenarios: slow request 1 followed by fast request 2; failing request 0; then explicit cancellation of request 1.
Expect session-2 in both result and the actor store; show "Could not load practice data" after failure and "Load cancelled" after explicit cancellation.

checks.label: Latest async request wins in display and actor

quiz.question: What prevents an older response from replacing the newest result?
choices: Checking that its request ID is still current
Storing the response in a String
quiz.explanation: The request ID ties each response to the request that is still active.

hints: Keep a monotonically increasing request ID.
Cancel the old task and capture the new ID before starting the Task.
After awaiting, check cancellation and confirm the captured ID still matches before changing visible data.

math.explanation: State transitions and event ordering: List valid transitions and reason about two possible orders of asynchronous events.
math.question: Two requests start in order: A has ID 4, B has ID 5. B completes, then A. Which value should remain visible, and why?
choices: B, because only ID 5 is current
math.feedback: Keep B. Once ID 5 is current, the late ID 4 result fails the current-request check.

externalNotes: Uses actual top-level async Swift, Task scheduling, actor storage, and supplied race/failure/cancellation scenarios. The Mac companion must compile and run this code using a compatible Apple toolchain. Run it in Xcode as well when attaching a real interface; browser execution cannot replace that Apple environment.

title: Save a durable practice log
summary: Separate the practice model from storage, save entries as JSON, and recover safely from bad data.
explanation: Persistence means keeping information outside the running program so it can be loaded later. A variable in memory normally disappears when the process ends. A file can remain on disk, but only if you write it to an appropriate location and keep that file. Separate the model, which describes an entry's information, from storage functions, which encode, write, read, and decode it. The screen can then use the result without being responsible for every file operation. This separation also makes success and recovery easier to inspect.

Codable combines Encodable and Decodable. Swift can generate their behavior for a struct whose stored properties also support them. JSONEncoder().encode(original) constructs an encoder and asks it to turn the array into Data. JSONDecoder().decode([ReadingEntry].self, from: bytes) names the exact expected type and converts bytes back. .self here refers to the type itself as an argument; it is not an array instance. The brackets in [ReadingEntry] mean an array of that model. If the bytes have a different shape or wrong field types, decoding can throw rather than producing valid entries.

throws on a function announces that it can fail. try marks the possibly failing operation. do groups operations whose errors you want to handle, and catch runs when one throws. Return a clear result in both success and failure paths. A LoadResult can contain an entries array and a message. On damaged input, returning an empty collection plus a message containing could not be read makes recovery visible without crashing. Do not use try! for this case: it assumes success and would turn a decoding failure into a crash. A controlled fallback should not silently overwrite the damaged file before a real app's recovery policy is decided.

options: .atomic asks Data to write through an auxiliary file and replace the destination on success, reducing the risk of exposing a partly written destination. Atomic means one indivisible update at that file-replacement level; it does not turn several separate files or read-modify-write operations into a transaction. Two writers can still overwrite each other's changes without coordination. A consistency invariant is something that should stay true through valid operations. Moving three of twelve entries from planned to done should keep twelve total. A crash after deleting them but before inserting them elsewhere can violate that total if the change is split into unrelated writes.

Overloading means functions can share a name when their input signatures differ. loadEntries(_ data: Data) loads supplied bytes; loadEntries(from url: URL) reads the file and then reuses the byte decoder. The underscore lets the Data call omit a label, while from is the URL call's label. Data("broken".utf8) makes bytes from the letters of broken using UTF-8 text encoding. Those bytes are not valid JSON for [PracticeEntry], so they should exercise the catch path. A file-read failure and a decode failure are different causes, but both need an understandable outcome.

For the exercise, use Codable PracticeEntry values, encode the supplied Swift/20 entry, save atomically at the supplied temporary file URL, and load it through the URL function. Return an empty collection and a could not be read message for the broken-byte fixture. The checks establish file round-tripping and controlled malformed-data recovery within one run. The companion removes its sandbox after runs, so this does not demonstrate survival across app restarts. In a real Xcode app, use an appropriate persistent application-support location and test stop/relaunch separately; old file formats may also need migrations, meaning deliberate conversion to a new format. Foundation compilation must succeed on the compatible Apple toolchain, and the fixture's documented cold compile limit may still prevent verification in that companion.

analogy.familiar: A labeled archive box
analogy.connection: Persistence is like putting a labeled box on a shelf and opening it the next day.
analogy.limit: A shelf can contain a damaged label or an old format, so loading still needs an error path.

steps: Define a Codable PracticeEntry value.
Encode [PracticeEntry(title: "Swift", minutes: 20)], save it atomically to the supplied temporary file URL, and load it through loadEntries(from:).
Decode Data("broken".utf8) through loadEntries(_:). Return an empty collection and a message containing "could not be read".

quiz.question: Why should decoding be inside a `do`/`catch`?
choices: Saved bytes may be malformed or incompatible
quiz.explanation: Decoding can throw, so the app should handle a failed load deliberately.

hints: Make the entry Codable so JSONEncoder and JSONDecoder can work with it.
Return a LoadResult in both the success and catch paths.
Try `JSONDecoder().decode([PracticeEntry].self, from: data)` and use `Data("broken".utf8)` to exercise recovery.

math.explanation: Consistency invariants: Prove the conserved total for a valid update and check interrupted and concurrent cases.
math.question: A tracker has 12 saved entries. One valid operation moves 3 entries from the “planned” group to “done.” How many total entries should exist afterward, and what failure case could break the invariant?
choices: 9; deleting planned entries is always expected
12; a crash between delete and insert could break it
math.feedback: A move preserves the total at 12. If the two writes are not atomic, interruption between them can lose or duplicate entries.

externalNotes: The companion deletes its sandbox directory after each run, so this exercise checks atomic disk round-tripping and malformed-data recovery within one run. To verify survival across app restarts, inject an application-support URL in an Xcode app, save an entry, stop the app, and launch again. Plan versioning/migration separately; the temporary companion fixture does not establish persistent iOS storage. This Foundation-dependent lesson may hit the companion's 30-second cold compile limit on the development toolchain; compilation and execution have not yet been verified there.

title: Check a large list fairly
summary: Test a search function and compare work counts for two input sizes under the same rules.
explanation: A test compares an observable result with an expected one. Good search tests ask more than “did one name show up?” Test an item at the beginning, one at the end, and a value that is absent. These cases make the search do different amounts of work and catch different mistakes. A linear search checks entries one after another until it finds a match or reaches the end. Linear describes how its worst-case work grows with the number of entries. Count comparisons so you can explain the work, rather than relying on one stopwatch result.

Array positions start at zero. The first entry has index 0, the second index 1, and so on. Position is different from value: [4, 8, 12, 16] has 12 at position 2. Int? allows a returned index to be a whole number or nil when no position was found. values.enumerated() supplies a sequence of pairs containing the offset and value. for (index, value) unpacks each pair, a tuple, into two names. In this array example, the enumeration offsets are valid array indices. That assumption should not be carried over blindly to other collection types.

Increase comparisons once for each equality question about an entry, before possibly returning on a match. That makes a first-item match count one instead of zero. return exits the function as soon as it finds the target, so later entries are not compared. If the loop finishes, return nil with the total number inspected. For an empty array there are no loop turns, so the missing result has zero comparisons. If duplicate targets exist, this search returns the first one it encounters. The function's behavior and the counting rules should be explicit before measuring it.

Array(0..<6) turns the half-open range into [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. The six-item last-target search makes six comparisons; the twelve-item last-target search makes twelve. Doubling this input doubles its counted work. For a missing value, every item must also be checked. In general a linear scan can do about n comparisons in the worst case, where n means the number of entries. Growing from 500 to 2,000 entries multiplies the size by 2,000 ÷ 500 = 4, so comparable worst-case work is four times as large. A first-item match can still take just one comparison at either size.

Elapsed time depends on more than algorithm work. Other programs, hardware, compiler settings, warm-up, and the test environment can change a timing. A comparison count is repeatable for this same algorithm and input, though it does not account for every cost. For a fair before-and-after optimization comparison, keep the same list, same query, and same expected answer, then change the method being compared. If a prebuilt index speeds up later lookups, include the work and memory needed to construct and maintain it. Counting fewer comparisons does not prove every part of an app became fast.

For the supplied find function, return SearchResult with an optional index and comparison count. Use Array(0..<100) for the sample, store smallRun for 99, largeRun for 199 in 200 entries, and missingRun for -1 in the sample. Expect indices 99, 199, and nil with counts 100, 200, and 100; finding 0 takes one comparison. The checks cover last match, missing input, doubled work, and first match. The fixture measures growth under two sizes, not an optimized before-and-after UI. Explain those limits, run the core behavior checks, and use equivalent conditions if you later compare another implementation in the Apple environment.

analogy.familiar: Finding a name in a roster
analogy.connection: A linear search checks one roster entry at a time until it finds the name.
analogy.limit: A comparison count explains work for this algorithm; it does not predict every source of elapsed time.

steps: Write a search function that returns an index and comparison count.
Try the first item 0, last item 99, and missing item -1 in Array(0..<100). Expect indexes 0, 99, and nil.
Store smallRun for target 99 in 100 entries, largeRun for target 199 in 200 entries, and missingRun for -1 in 100 entries. Expect 100, 200, and 100 comparisons.

checks.label: First item takes one comparison
checks.expression: find(0, in: sample).index == 0 && find(0, in: sample).comparisons == 1

quiz.question: Why count comparisons as well as time?
choices: The count is less affected by unrelated computer activity
Comparison counts prove every program is fast
quiz.explanation: A work count is repeatable for the same input and algorithm, while wall-clock timing can vary.

hints: Use `enumerated()` to get both the position and value.
Increase the comparison count once for each value checked.
For a missing target, finish with a nil index and the full comparison count.

math.explanation: Algorithm growth and measurement: Compare work as input size grows and distinguish theoretical growth from one timing result.
math.question: A linear scan checks n items in the worst case. If n grows from 500 to 2,000, about how many times as many comparisons should it perform?
math.feedback: The input is four times larger, so a linear scan performs about four times as many comparisons. One timing measurement can still vary.

externalNotes: The fixture compares a linear scan across two input sizes under identical last-item conditions. That measures growth, not an optimized before/after UI. For an optimization comparison, hold one list/query fixed and compare counted linear-scan work with a prebuilt index; include index construction cost and confirm identical results.

title: Type a score card
summary: Give player data clear types and format a small score summary.
explanation:
TypeScript is JavaScript with extra descriptions of the kinds of values your code expects. A compiler checks those descriptions before producing JavaScript to run. number describes numbers such as 14; string describes text such as '14'; boolean describes true or false. Quoted '14' is text even though it looks like a number. These differences help catch mistakes before you see a broken screen.

For example, a numeric score that gains 5 points and then 2 more becomes 5 + 2 = 7. Subtracting 2 from 5 gives 3; multiplying 5 by 2 gives 10. JavaScript uses +, -, and * for those numeric operations. Choosing number makes that arithmetic intention clear.

Read the punctuation as instructions. The colon after a field gives its type; runner: Runner gives the parameter's type; ): string says the function returns text. Parentheses hold a function's inputs. return sends a result back to its caller. runner.name uses a dot to read a field. Backticks start a template string, and ${...} inserts the value of the expression inside. Curly braces describe an object or enclose the function body, depending on their location.

An object with laps: '9' does not meet Runner because that value is text. To practice type errors, temporarily change a numeric laps value to quoted text and run the full compiler check. Expect a reported error, then restore the number. A runtime test that checks the sentence is useful but does not establish that the compiler rejects incorrect types.

In the exercise, Player has name: string and score: number. scoreSummary accepts a Player and must return a sentence in the form name has score points. Include the final period and spaces. The player, summary, and function names connect to the supplied checks. Reading player.score gives the actual score, while the text 'player.score' would literally print those characters.

Types disappear from the JavaScript that runs. An interface cannot clean or validate a network response. If unchecked outside data says score is '12', the runtime still receives text unless you check it. Keep compile-time checking and runtime validation distinct. For this fixture the values are already supplied correctly, so concentrate on the typed function and formatting.

analogy.familiar: A labeled score sheet
analogy.connection: An interface is like a score sheet with named spaces and expected kinds of entries.
analogy.limit: A typed sheet helps while writing code; an external value still needs runtime checking.

steps: Define a Player interface with name and score.
Write a function that formats one player into a summary.
Use player { name: "Mina", score: 12 }; summary should be "Mina has 12 points." Try Bo with score 3 as a second case.

quiz.question: Which type should describe `score: 12`?
quiz.explanation: TypeScript uses `number` for numeric values.

hints: The score is numeric, so declare it as `number`.
Return one template string from the function.
Include both `player.name` and `player.score` in the summary.

math.explanation: Addition, subtraction, and multiplication: Calculate one small example by hand, then compare it with the program result.
math.question: A player earns 4 points and then 3 more. What is the total?
math.feedback: Add 4 and 3 to get 7.

externalNotes: Type-error practice: after the valid solution compiles, temporarily append this line and run the full TypeScript check: scoreSummary({ name: "Mina", score: "12" }); The compiler should report an error. Remove the line before completing the lesson. Runtime checks alone cannot establish rejection of an incorrect type.

title: Describe activities with types
summary: Combine aliases, unions, intersections, and interfaces to model different activity records.
explanation: A type alias gives a reusable name to a type: type Size = 'small' | 'large'. The | means either choice, called a union. The quoted values are literal types: exactly those words, rather than any string. An intersection uses & to require both sets of fields. An interface also describes an object shape. These tools let us describe related records without losing their differences.

The shared kind field tells us which shape we have. A discriminated union is a union whose members carry distinct identifying literal values. Narrowing means a check gives TypeScript a more specific type for one part of the code. Checking session.kind === 'draw' proves that this branch has pictures. In the other branch, the only remaining member is Singing, with songs.

A separate alias containing more words does not automatically add more shapes to a union. In your starter, ActivityKind includes walk, read, and code, but Activity contains only WalkActivity | ReadActivity. There is no CodeActivity in that union yet. Follow the actual accepted parameter type when deciding which branches describe is responsible for.

For two sets of activity names, {walk, read} and {read, code}, the overlap is {read}; their union is {walk, read, code}. This set vocabulary explains either/shared choices. An object type intersection uses & to require all fields from both object types, so do not read it as keeping only the fields the objects share.

For the exercise, both branches must include title and minutes. The walk branch reads steps; the read branch reads pages. Preserve the punctuation shown by the requested sentences. Checking kind before reading a branch-specific field teaches both the compiler and the reader why that field is available. Do not convert all fields to text as a substitute for describing the correct shape.

After your valid version compiles, temporarily try a walk record with pages and no steps. The compiler should reject it, because the discriminant and fields do not agree. Remove the invalid example afterward. These are development checks; a forged network object can still lie at runtime, so outside data needs actual value checks before it becomes a trusted Activity.

analogy.familiar: Activity badges
analogy.connection: A union is like choosing one badge from a small set, while an intersection means an item must satisfy both descriptions.
analogy.limit: A union does not mean an object can freely omit required fields; each branch still has its own shape.

steps: Create an ActivityKind alias for walk, read, or code.
Define a common activity interface and two specific shapes.
Use walk { kind: "walk", title: "Park", minutes: 20, steps: 1800 } and reading { kind: "read", title: "Novel", minutes: 15, pages: 8 }. Include 1800 steps and 8 pages in the respective summaries.

quiz.question: What lets TypeScript narrow `Activity` in the `if`?
quiz.explanation: A check of a shared literal discriminant narrows the union to the matching branch.

hints: The common `kind` property identifies which shape is present.
When kind is walk, `steps` exists; otherwise this union branch is read.
Return a separate message for each branch and include the matching numeric detail.

math.explanation: Sets and overlap: Draw or list shared, distinct, and missing members of two small collections.
math.question: Set A has {walk, read}; set B has {read, code}. What is their overlap?
math.feedback: The shared member in both sets is read.

externalNotes: Type-error practice: after the valid solution compiles, temporarily append this line and run the full TypeScript check: const invalidActivity: Activity = { kind: "walk", title: "Park", minutes: 20, pages: 8 }; The compiler should report an error. Remove the line before completing the lesson. Runtime checks alone cannot establish rejection of an incorrect type.

title: Calculate typed practice rewards
summary: Use an enum, class, and typed function to calculate points from practice minutes.
explanation: An enum gives names to a set of values. A function can use those named values as a typed input. A class describes objects that keep data and provide actions, called methods. Each learner object can keep its own points. A method can call a reward function so the calculation stays in one place instead of being repeated in every update.

Practice.Drawing and Practice.Singing are named enum members. A plain numeric enum assigns 0 to the first member and 1 to the next unless values are specified. Those values identify activity categories; they are not point multipliers. The current reward rule is the same for both categories, so kind is accepted but does not change the calculation. Do not invent a bonus that the task did not request.

TypeScript infers points as number from its initial 0. The typed method requires numeric minutes and an enum activity, then promises a number result. A different Student starts with its own 0; two students do not share the points field. Store updates on this.points instead of a temporary local variable that disappears when the method returns.

In the exercise, award the first session's reward and accumulate the second reward too. Twenty minutes earns 2; fifteen earns 1; learner.points should then be 3. Keep earned and secondEarned as the names used by the checks. Returning the total from the second call would produce 3 rather than the requested session reward 1.

Temporarily passing quoted minutes such as '20' should fail the full TypeScript check. Restore a number afterward. Numeric typing alone does not ensure minutes is nonnegative or finite; the supplied exercise assumes valid durations. For real outside input you would validate that range too. Math.floor is rounding down, so negative values are another reason not to treat type checking as validation.

analogy.familiar: A punch card
analogy.connection: The class is like a learner’s punch card, and the reward function decides how many marks one session earns.
analogy.limit: The rules in this small model are practice rules, not a universal measure of learning.

steps: Define Activity.Coding and Activity.Reading. For both activities, reward one point for each complete 10 minutes; discard a partial block.
Create a learner class with an award method.
Use learner.award(20, Activity.Coding) for earned and learner.award(15, Activity.Reading) for secondEarned. Expect 2, 1, and a stored total of 3.

quiz.question: What does `Math.floor(15 / 10)` return?
quiz.explanation: Floor rounds down to the nearest whole number, so the result is 1.

hints: The enum names the kind of activity; the sample reward depends on minutes.
Use `Math.floor(minutes / 10)` to count each complete ten-minute block.
Add the reward to `this.points`, then return the amount just gained.

math.explanation: Functions and input-output relationships: Make a small input-output table and check it against the function.
math.question: The rule gives 1 point per complete 10 minutes. How many for 30 minutes?
math.feedback: There are three complete ten-minute blocks in 30 minutes.

externalNotes: Type-error practice: after the valid solution compiles, temporarily append this line and run the full TypeScript check: learner.award("20", Activity.Coding); The compiler should report an error. Remove the line before completing the lesson. Runtime checks alone cannot establish rejection of an incorrect type.

title: Keep collection types reusable
summary: Create a generic collection that preserves the item type for both numbers and text.
explanation: A generic lets one piece of code work with different types while remembering which type was chosen. The type parameter T is a placeholder for a type, not a runtime value. Collection<number> chooses number; Collection<string> chooses string. Both can use the same storage and methods, while TypeScript checks which values can go into each instance.

private asks TypeScript to prevent outside code from directly using values; callers use the methods. This TypeScript private keyword is not a security boundary for secret data at runtime. void means add does not promise a useful returned value. first returns T | undefined because an empty array has no first item. undefined means absent, rather than the number zero or an empty string.

The same methods keep their chosen return types: counts.first() is number | undefined, while colors.first() is string | undefined. Replacing T with any would lose that connection and hide wrong-type mistakes. A bare new Collection() can still represent an empty collection, but an explicit type parameter is clearer when choosing the values you plan to store.

For the exercise, add must push into this.values, and first must return this.values[0]. Set firstNumber from numbers.first() and firstWord from words.first(). With the supplied inputs those values are 7 and maple. Adding does not replace the earlier item, so the first value stays first after later additions. Do not invent a default when the collection is empty.

After the valid solution compiles, temporarily try numbers.add('seven'). Expect a compiler error, then remove that call. A generic class provides compile-time consistency; it does not inspect unknown network values by itself. Check untrusted values before calling add. Distinguishing an empty collection from one containing 0 or empty text is part of preserving the actual stored value.

analogy.familiar: A box with a label
analogy.connection: A generic collection is like a box labeled with the kind of item it accepts.
analogy.limit: The label guides checked code, but it does not inspect unknown JSON at runtime.

steps: Define `Collection<T>` with an internal array.
Add an `add` method and a `first` method.
Add 7 to Collection<number> and "maple" to Collection<string>; assign firstNumber and firstWord from first(). An empty Collection<boolean> returns undefined.

quiz.question: What does `T` represent in `Collection<T>`?
choices: A type supplied when the collection is created
quiz.explanation: The type parameter stands for the element type chosen by the caller.

hints: The internal array should be `T[]`.
Use `push` to keep the supplied value.
Return `this.values[0]`; its type includes undefined because a collection may be empty.

math.explanation: Logical constraints and correctness: State the assumptions, derive valid cases, and find a counterexample to an invalid assumption.
math.question: A generic `first<T>` returns the first element or undefined. Which statement is always safe without extra assumptions?
choices: If the collection is empty, the result may be undefined
The result is always a number
The result must equal the last item
math.feedback: The type is preserved as T when present, but an empty collection has no first value.

externalNotes: Type-error practice: after the valid solution compiles, temporarily append this line and run the full TypeScript check: numbers.add("seven"); The compiler should report an error. Remove the line before completing the lesson. Runtime checks alone cannot establish rejection of an incorrect type.

title: Connect event names to payloads
summary: Use mapped and conditional types so each event name carries its matching payload.
explanation: An event is a value describing something that happened. Its type field names the event, and its payload holds that event's details. One event might carry a title; another might carry a percentage. A useful type keeps the name paired with the correct details. Merely allowing either name and either payload independently would allow incorrect combinations.

K extends keyof Details means K must be one of those allowed keys. A conditional type has the form condition ? typeIfTrue : typeIfFalse. never describes an impossible type with no valid values. In PayloadFor<K>, the valid key selects Details[K]. Because K is already constrained to keyof Details, the condition is always satisfied for allowed uses; it still shows the conditional-type syntax.

Read the mapped type in stages. [K in keyof Details] visits each key while building a type. At selected it builds {type: 'selected'; payload: {label: string}}. At counted it builds the matching count shape. The final [keyof Details] takes the built property types and combines them into a union. Each union member still contains its correctly paired name and payload.

Checking event.type === 'selected' narrows DemoEvent to its selected member, so event.payload.label is known to exist there. In the remaining branch, counted's count is available. Trying a selected event with only count fails the compiler. You can understand or expand the mapped declaration into two explicit union members; the reusable form is useful when the key list grows.

The exercise calls its map Payloads, with opened/title and progress/percent. Keep those names, build AppEvent from the mapped union, and format the opened and progress sentences exactly. The % in a template string is ordinary displayed punctuation after the percentage; it is not an arithmetic remainder operator there. The mapping preserves relationships, not where an event came from at runtime.

Temporarily pair opened with {percent: 50} and run the full TypeScript check to see a rejection, then remove the invalid call. Types are erased at runtime, so real incoming events still require validation. An event with a numeric percent also needs a separate range rule if you intend to require 0 through 100; the current type number alone does not impose that rule.

analogy.familiar: Mail labels and contents
analogy.connection: The event name is a label that tells the receiver what kind of message is inside.
analogy.limit: A label only helps when the payload actually follows the declared shape; validate external messages at runtime too.

steps: Describe the payload for each event name.
Map each key into a matching `{ type, payload }` member.
Handle opened with title "Notes" as "Opened Notes", and progress with percent 50 as "Progress 50%".

quiz.question: What does the mapped type preserve?
choices: The relationship between each key and its payload
Only the number of event keys
The runtime source of every event
quiz.explanation: The mapped union builds each event member from a key and that key’s corresponding payload.

hints: The mapped type loops over `keyof Payloads`.
Each member should have `type: K` and `payload: Payloads[K]`.
Narrow using `event.type`, then read only the field for that case.

math.explanation: Logical constraints and correctness: State the assumptions, derive valid cases, and find a counterexample to an invalid assumption.
math.question: A `progress` event requires `{percent: number}` and an `opened` event requires `{title: string}`. Which is a valid counterexample to a system that checks only the event name?
math.feedback: The first pair has a valid name but the wrong payload, showing why the name and payload relationship matters.

externalNotes: Type-error practice: after the valid solution compiles, temporarily append this line and run the full TypeScript check: handle({ type: "opened", payload: { percent: 50 } }); The compiler should report an error. Remove the line before completing the lesson. Runtime checks alone cannot establish rejection of an incorrect type.

title: Validate data at runtime
summary: Treat API data as unknown until checks confirm the fields and ranges you need.
explanation: Outside data can be wrong even when your program has good TypeScript types. Runtime means the time when JavaScript actually executes. TypeScript's types are erased before then. Use unknown for an unchecked value: you must narrow it before reading fields or doing calculations. any instead disables many checks and can let a missing field go unnoticed.

typeof returns a value's basic runtime kind. JavaScript reports typeof null as 'object', so we explicitly reject null before using in. The in operator checks whether a named property exists. ! means not, || means either condition is enough, and && requires every condition. Early return false stops before an unsafe field access. This code requires known fields but permits extra fields; it does not require a particular object prototype.

NaN means not-a-number, but typeof NaN is 'number'. Infinity is also a number in JavaScript but is not a finite measurement. Number.isFinite rejects both, and does not convert numeric text into a number. A >= 0 test excludes negatives and includes zero. This guard permits nonnegative fractions because the task requires a number, not specifically an integer.

If a separate contract says durations must also be at most 600, add value.minutes <= 600 to the finite nonnegative check. Then 0 and 45 pass that range, Infinity fails, and 601 fails the upper bound. The exercise's current PracticeResponse contract requires finite nonnegative minutes without that extra upper bound; the matching math question describes the stricter hypothetical range.

For the exercise, validate PracticeResponse's title and minutes. Reject null, a missing title or minutes field, wrong field types, negative minutes, NaN, and Infinity. Accept the supplied good object. A type assertion such as value as PracticeResponse would only tell the compiler to trust you; it would perform none of these actual runtime checks.

Temporarily read unvalidated.minutes from an unknown value without a guard, then run the full TypeScript check. It should fail. Remove that practice line afterward. unknown does not itself validate anything; it makes unchecked use a compiler error. Your guard's runtime code is what determines whether the data really has a string title and a finite nonnegative duration.

analogy.familiar: Checking a parcel
analogy.connection: Runtime validation is like checking a parcel label and contents before signing that it is yours.
analogy.limit: A shape check only proves the conditions it tests; add checks for any rule your app depends on.

steps: Describe the expected response.
Write a type guard for object, title, and non-negative minutes.
Use good { title: "Swift", minutes: 20 }, missing { title: "Swift" }, and wrong { title: "Swift", minutes: "20" }. Also reject null, negative minutes, NaN, and Infinity.

checks.label: Null, invalid ranges, and non-finite values are rejected

quiz.question: Why use `unknown` for unchecked API data?
choices: It requires a runtime check before use
quiz.explanation: `unknown` prevents using a value until code narrows it with checks.

hints: Check that the value is a non-null object first.
Use `in` to verify both property names exist.
Check title is a string and minutes is a finite non-negative number.

math.explanation: Sets of valid values and validation constraints: Define valid external values and produce counterexamples for missing validation.
math.question: A valid API value must have a string title and a finite minutes number from 0 to 600. Which value must be rejected?
math.feedback: Infinity is numeric in JavaScript but not finite, so a range check alone is not enough.

externalNotes: Type-error practice: after the valid solution compiles, temporarily append this line and run the full TypeScript check: const unvalidated: unknown = { title: "Swift", minutes: 20 }; const unsafeMinutes = unvalidated.minutes; The compiler should report an error. Remove the line before completing the lesson. Runtime checks alone cannot establish rejection of an incorrect type.

title: Model a cancellable workflow
summary: Represent each workflow phase as a typed state and ignore results from outdated requests.
explanation: An asynchronous job can finish later, after other code has run. A workflow needs to describe what is happening now: idle, loading, success, error, or cancelled. A discriminated union lets each kind of state carry just the fields it needs. Success has data; error has a message; idle does not pretend to have either.

A reducer is a function that receives the current state and an action, then returns the next state. The action describes an event; it does not edit state by itself. A requestId identifies one attempt. If request 8 starts after request 7, the reply from 7 should no longer control the screen, even when it arrives last.

The order of the branches matters. start may begin a new loading state from any state. Every other action needs a current loading state and matching requestId. The || means either a wrong state kind or wrong id is enough to ignore it. Checking state.kind first also safely narrows state before reading its requestId. resolve produces success; reject produces error; the remaining valid action is cancel.

For the exercise, keep the supplied State and Action unions. reduce should return the exact same state on stale or invalid terminal actions, because the checks compare object identity with ===. Accept only the active request's result, rejection, or cancellation. An idle state must ignore resolve. Once cancelled, even the matching late resolve must be ignored because the state is no longer loading.

Trace the matching math case: loading request 8 first receives resolve for 7. That id mismatch keeps loading 8 unchanged. Then reject for 8 matches, so the final state is error for 8. The order of arrival alone does not choose the winner; current identity does.

The supplied first request uses id 2. Its matching success carries ['book']; id 1 is stale. Add or retain the current and stale variables required by the checks. Temporarily construct success without data and run the full TypeScript check to see why success needs that field, then remove the invalid line. This reducer models transitions; it does not itself fetch data or schedule requests.

analogy.familiar: A package tracking page
analogy.connection: A workflow state is like one current package status: it is waiting, moving, delivered, or delayed.
analogy.limit: A status page should not let an old tracking update replace a newer one.

steps: Define a union for idle, loading, success, error, and cancelled.
Write a reducer for start, resolve, reject, and cancel actions.
Start request 2 from idle, resolve request 2 with ["book"], and try resolving stale request 1 with ["old"]. Also reject and cancel request 2, then ignore a result after cancellation.

checks.label: Current rejection becomes error
checks.expression: (() => { const failed = reduce(loading, {type:"reject",requestId:2,message:"Offline"}); return failed.kind === "error" && failed.message === "Offline"; })()

checks.label: Cancellation prevents late success
checks.expression: (() => { const cancelled = reduce(loading, {type:"cancel",requestId:2}); return cancelled.kind === "cancelled" && reduce(cancelled,{type:"resolve",requestId:2,data:["late"]}) === cancelled; })()

quiz.question: What should happen when an old request resolves after a newer one?
choices: Replace the new result with old data
quiz.explanation: Only the currently active request ID should be allowed to update the workflow.

hints: Handle start before requiring a current loading state.
For other actions, compare the current state request ID with the action ID.
Return the unchanged state for a mismatch, then map matching actions to success/error/cancelled.

math.explanation: State transitions and event ordering: List valid transitions and reason about two possible orders of asynchronous events.
math.question: Request 8 is loading. A resolve for request 7 arrives, then a reject for request 8. What is the final state?
math.feedback: The stale resolve is ignored; the matching reject moves the active request to error.

externalNotes: Type-error practice: after the valid solution compiles, temporarily append this line and run the full TypeScript check: const invalidState: State = { kind: "success", requestId: 2 }; The compiler should report an error. Remove the line before completing the lesson. Runtime checks alone cannot establish rejection of an incorrect type.

title: Build a profile from components
summary: Compose a profile from a component, pass details as props, and update a local counter.
explanation:
React builds interfaces from components. A component is a function that returns a description of what should appear. JSX is the HTML-like notation inside JavaScript, such as

Hello

. A JSX-aware runner translates it before execution. These examples use the lesson's available React object; they need React and JSX support, so they cannot be pasted unchanged into a plain JavaScript console.

Capitalized <Profile ... /> asks React to use your component; lowercase <section> describes a built-in HTML element. name="Tara" passes text. Curly braces inside JSX evaluate JavaScript: {props.name} inserts the actual name. Text outside braces, such as Learning, appears literally. The closing /> means this component call has no enclosed children. A returned tree needs one surrounding element, here main.

State is data React remembers between renders. A render is React calling components to work out the current interface. setTaps asks React to render with the updated state; it does not directly rewrite the button's HTML. The arrow () => ... creates a function for a future click. Passing that function matters: calling setTaps while building the screen would update during rendering instead of waiting for the user.

current => current + 1 is a functional update: React supplies the latest queued count. Calling setCount(count + 1) also works for the exercise's separate clicks, but functional updates help when several increments are queued together. An ordinary local let variable would reset when the function runs again and would not itself tell React to render. Call hooks such as useState at the top level of the component, not inside a condition.

For the exercise, preserve Mina's Swift profile and the Practice button's label. Each click increments only count. Starting from 0, three taps follow 0 → 1 → 2 → 3; adding one each time is counting, not multiplication. A changing counter should not change read-only profile props. In larger apps, define child components outside their parent to preserve stable component identity; the starter's nested Profile is adequate for this simple stateless example.

analogy.familiar: A name badge and tally
analogy.connection: Props are like the name printed on a badge; state is like a tally you can change while using the page.
analogy.limit: A component should not change its incoming props, just as a guest should not rewrite a printed badge.

steps: Create Profile with name "Mina" and subject "Swift". Render Mina as an h2 and "Learning Swift" in a paragraph.
Start count at 0 and display "Practice taps: 0". Label the counter button "Practice".
Increase count once per click. Two clicks should show "Practice taps: 2" while the profile text stays the same.

checks.label: Two clicks increment only the counter
checks.expression: (async () => { const button = document.querySelector("button"); if (!button) return false; button.click(); await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 20)); button.click(); await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 20)); return document.querySelector("main")?.textContent.includes("Practice taps: 2") && document.querySelector("h2")?.textContent === "Mina"; })()

quiz.question: What causes the counter display to update after `setCount`?
choices: React schedules a render with the new state
The button changes its own HTML directly
quiz.explanation: The state setter tells React to render using the updated state value.

hints: Keep `name` and `subject` as props on Profile.
Use the setter returned by `useState`.
Pass `() => setCount(count + 1)` to the button’s onClick.

math.explanation: Counting and simple sequences: Count the items or steps and predict the next value.
math.question: The counter starts at 0 and you tap 3 times. What is the next count?
math.feedback: Three increments from zero produce 3.

title: Build an activity board
summary: Handle a labeled form, reject empty submissions, and show each valid entry once.
explanation: React handles actions through event-handler functions. A controlled input takes its displayed value from state and updates that state when someone types. value sets the displayed text; onChange tells React how to respond to edits. You need both. A visible label tells people what the field is for, including people using assistive technology.

Forms normally submit by navigating or reloading the page. event.preventDefault() prevents that default action so your React code can handle submission. It does not stop typing. trim() removes whitespace from both ends of a string. Three spaces become empty text, whose length is 0. A valid submission here needs trimmed length greater than 0, so a blank draft must be rejected before anything is added.

The early return stops the invalid path. [...current, cleaned] creates a new array by spreading the existing items, then appending the cleaned text. It preserves earlier notes and gives React a new value to render. map visits each note and returns one li element. key helps React track list children; an index key is acceptable for this simple append-only list, but stable unique ids are better for lists that reorder or remove items.

role="status" exposes the message as status feedback for assistive technology. type="submit" connects the button to the form's submit action, so pressing Enter in the field can also submit. Attach addition to the form handler once; adding in both an onClick and onSubmit can duplicate items. The handler receives a function reference submit, rather than submit(), which would run immediately.

For the exercise, the field label is Activity, the button is Add activity, and the required messages are Enter an activity first. and Activity added. Keep those words because the checks inspect visible behavior. Reject a blank or whitespace-only draft, add a valid trimmed item exactly once, then clear draft. Clearing a message alone does not clear the input: the controlled field follows its own state.

analogy.familiar: A sign-up clipboard
analogy.connection: A controlled field is like a clipboard where the displayed text follows the current form value.
analogy.limit: A form should keep its label visible so people know what belongs in the field.

steps: Track draft text, message, and submitted activities with state.
Add a labeled input and form submit handler.
An empty submit must add no row and show "Enter an activity first." Enter "  Read  ", submit once, and expect one Read row, a cleared field, and "Activity added."

checks.label: Empty and valid submissions behave correctly
checks.expression: (async () => { const form = document.querySelector("form"), input = document.querySelector("input"); if (!form || !input) return false; form.dispatchEvent(new Event("submit", {bubbles:true,cancelable:true})); await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 20)); if (document.querySelectorAll("li").length !== 0 || document.querySelector("[role=status]")?.textContent !== "Enter an activity first.") return false; Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(HTMLInputElement.prototype,"value").set.call(input,"  Read  "); input.dispatchEvent(new Event("input",{bubbles:true})); await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r,20)); form.dispatchEvent(new Event("submit",{bubbles:true,cancelable:true})); await new Promise(r=>setTimeout(r,20)); return document.querySelectorAll("li").length === 1 && document.querySelector("li")?.textContent === "Read" && input.value === "" && document.querySelector("[role=status]")?.textContent === "Activity added."; })()

quiz.question: Why call `event.preventDefault()` on form submit?
choices: To prevent a page reload while handling the form in React
quiz.explanation: Preventing the browser’s default submit navigation lets the React handler update the page state.

hints: Trim the draft before checking whether it is blank.
Use a functional state update to append to the current list.
On valid text, append once, clear the draft, and set a success message.

math.explanation: Compound conditions and cases: Check combinations of conditions, including boundary and empty cases.
math.question: A form accepts text only when its trimmed length is greater than 0. Is three spaces valid?
choices: Yes, because the original length is 3
No, trimming leaves an empty string
math.feedback: Trimming removes the spaces, leaving no characters to submit.

title: Make a keyboard-friendly menu
summary: Build a menu with clear labels, keyboard actions, and predictable focus return.
explanation: Keyboard access means someone can use a feature without a mouse. Native buttons can receive focus with Tab and activate with Enter or Space. Focus is the control that currently receives keyboard input. Give buttons a visible name describing their action and keep focus visible. A clickable div would need extra keyboard behavior that a button already provides.

In JSX, {open && ...} renders the element when open is true. !value flips a boolean: false becomes true. We also need a deliberate focus plan. Opening should focus the first action after it exists; Escape should close and return focus to the trigger. A ref stores a reference to an actual DOM element without needing a render every time it changes.

useRef(null) starts without an element; React fills .current when the ref's button is mounted. ?. means only call focus when the current value exists. useEffect runs its work after React has committed the screen update, so the first button is available. [open] is the dependency array: run this effect when open changes. Setting a ref does not itself update the visible screen.

Key events bubble from a focused child to its ancestor, allowing nav's handler to see Escape from a list button. The close function hides the list and restores the trigger as the keyboard position. Tab is still ordinary focus navigation. This is a simple disclosure containing native buttons, not a full ARIA menu widget; adding role="menu" would require additional expected keyboard behavior such as arrow-key navigation.

For the exercise, the trigger's visible name must be Activities, aria-controls must point to activity-menu, and opening must focus Start practice. Escape closes and returns focus to Activities. Test it with Tab, Enter or Space, then Escape. Confirm the expanded attribute changes with state and focus really moves. This unit has no math question; the learning task is the interaction itself.

analogy.familiar: A labeled remote control
analogy.connection: A menu button is like a clearly labeled remote button that opens a small list of choices.
analogy.limit: A visible menu is not enough; keyboard users also need a clear path into and back out of it.

steps: Label the native trigger button "Activities", start aria-expanded at false, and set aria-controls to "activity-menu".
Show menu choices only while open and focus the first choice after opening.
Close with Escape and return focus to the menu button.

checks.label: Menu button has an accessible name
Opening focuses the first action; Escape closes and returns focus

title: Build a reading dashboard
summary: Use shared state and explicit loading, empty, error, and success views across dashboard screens.
explanation: A dashboard can show different views of one shared dataset. Store the selected view and loaded records in the common parent component so switching views preserves them. Home and Saved here are local screen choices; they do not change the browser URL or maintain separate saved records. The loader is a simulation, so no server or secret is needed.

Loading means waiting for a result. Empty means a successful result with no records. Error means the attempt failed. Success with records means the list is ready. Idle means no attempt yet. Treating all these cases as one blank list hides useful information. A role="alert" message can announce an error; a list of real results should appear only in the successful state.

++latest.current adds one and supplies that new number as this attempt's id. A ref retains this counter across renders without causing an extra render. setTimeout schedules the callback after a delay in milliseconds; 1,000 milliseconds is one second. Each callback keeps the id and mode from its own call. Before changing either results or errors, compare that id with the newest one.

Click Slow sample and then Error sample before the slow result arrives. The later error owns the current id, so its message remains; the old success is ignored. Reverse the kinds of outcomes and the same rule should protect a later success from an old error. For example, request 2 succeeds and request 1 later fails: keep request 2's success. Checking only successful responses would still let stale errors break the screen.

For your exercise, combine shared navigation with the loader and preserve the supplied labels and messages. Include Load sample, Load empty, Load error, and Load older slow result. Sample success shows A Field Guide; empty success says No books yet.; error says Books could not be loaded. Show Loading books… while waiting. Keep view independent of load state so Home/Saved preserves the current dataset. A real fetch loader must also check response status and guard both success and failure against stale ids.

analogy.connection: The dashboard is like a library desk that can show a shelf, a loading note, an empty shelf, or an explanation when the catalog is unavailable.
analogy.limit: Changing screens does not cancel a real request by itself; code must handle stale responses.

title: Explore a large list efficiently
summary: Filter a large fixed list, count examined rows, and preserve the same results while reducing repeated work.
explanation: Filtering a list examines each item to decide whether it matches. If there are n items and you inspect each once, that is linear work, written O(n). The O notation describes how work grows, not an exact clock time. Growing a list from 1,000 to 8,000 items means roughly eight times as many comparisons for the same full scan.

React may render again for a state update that does not affect the query or list. useMemo remembers a calculated result while its dependency values remain the same. A dependency is an input that can change the answer. It does not make a new query constant-time; a changed query still needs a scan. React compares each dependency with its previous value, so keeping the array itself stable matters too.

To compare work across renders, the exercise records each newly committed calculation result. A ref stores previous baseline and memoized object references and running counts. Its effect depends on the two result objects. If a result reference changed, add that result's examined count; then store the new references and put totals into state. The totals render does not change items, query, or repeat, so it does not create a measuring loop.

The exercise's list uses Array.from({length: 1000}, (_, i) => `Book ${i}`). It creates indexes 0 through 999; _ is a parameter name for an unused value and i is the index. Book 99 matches Book 99 and Book 990 through Book 999: 11 matches. slice(0, 10) displays the first ten without changing the full match array. Check every matching value as well as equal lengths: equal counts alone can hide different results.

Exclude repeat from the memoized dependencies but retain items and query. Initially each calculation represents 1,000 comparisons. After repeating unchanged inputs once, the baseline total becomes 2,000 while the memoized total stays 1,000, with identical match arrays. The check's totals assume this supplied run without development StrictMode. Extra development or discarded renders can make raw execution counts different. useMemo is a performance aid whose cache React may discard; correct results must not depend on retaining it.

analogy.familiar: Sorting a card box
analogy.connection: A list filter is like checking each card for a matching word; skipping a repeated check can save effort when the cards did not change.
analogy.limit: Memoization uses memory and only helps when the inputs repeat; it is not automatically faster for every small list.

steps: Keep the supplied 1,000 strings, Book 0 through Book 999, and initial query "Book 99". There are 11 matches; display the first 10.
Compare a baseline filter depending on query plus an unrelated repeat counter with a memoized filter depending only on items and query. Both filters count every examined item.

Add Repeat same search to change the unrelated counter. Record actual comparison totals after each calculation in an effect: one repeat should produce baseline total 2,000 and memoized total 1,000. Confirm that both filters still return identical matches.

Repeated render preserves results and avoids another memoized scan

math.feedback: A linear filter scales with item count, so eight times the items produce about eight times the checks.
