title: Test search races and failures
summary: Build a search view that ignores stale responses and keeps loading and error states understandable.
explanation: Asynchronous search can finish in a different order from when searches started. If A starts first but B finishes first, B may be the result the person now wants. A late success or failure from A must not replace it. Give each search a new id, store the latest id in a ref, and compare ids before applying either outcome.

In React, a controlled input keeps query in state. Each search handler uses the query from the render that supplied that handler. A callback created inside the handler keeps that snapshot, even if the person types a different query later. A request id decides whether the snapshot is still current. Typing alone need not start a request; pressing Search does in this exercise.

Check both race orders. Start a slow error, then a quick success: keep the success after the old error arrives. Start a slow success, then a quick error: keep the error and show no old list after the success arrives. Using the id check at the beginning of the callback protects both. Clearing error when a new search begins avoids displaying the old failure as though the new attempt already failed.

A useful interface test types into the actual input and activates the actual buttons, then waits long enough for the sample timers and inspects the visible outcome. It should cover loading, empty success, normal success, failure, and both stale-response orders. Testing only the existence of a search function or a particular variable name would miss a broken visible flow.

For the exercise, preserve Search books, Search, Fail search, Searching…, No results., and Search failed. Try again. Format successful rows as Result for followed by the captured query. A newer B success remains visible when older A fails; the math question is reasoning about event order, not calculating delay totals. The supplied timers simulate requests; replacing them with fetch requires the same current-id protection in both success and catch/error paths.

analogy.familiar: Two cooks finishing orders
analogy.connection: A request ID is like an order number that prevents an old plate from replacing the newest order at the table.
analogy.limit: The ID prevents stale display updates; it does not stop the network request from using time or resources.

Try again." && document.querySelectorAll("li").length===0; })()

title: A practice-session API
summary: Create routes for reading and adding practice entries in Express.
explanation: An API is an agreed way for programs to ask another program to do something. An HTTP request includes a method, a path, and sometimes a body of data. A route matches a method and path. GET /entries reads records; POST /entries asks to create one. A response has a status number and a body. JSON is a text format used to send objects and arrays between programs.

Number.isInteger requires a whole finite number, so it rejects a fraction, undefined, NaN, Infinity, and quoted numeric text. The bounds include 1 and 180; 0 and 181 fail. || means any invalid condition rejects the request. The default body = {} handles an omitted argument in this example. [...visits] makes a new array for the response, and push appends the valid record only after validation.

app.use installs middleware, code that runs before route handlers. express.json reads JSON request bodies, with a 20-kilobyte size limit. res.status chooses the status and res.json sends JSON. crypto.randomUUID creates a unique record identifier in this Node environment. A 200 means the read succeeded; 201 means a record was created; 400 asks the caller to fix invalid input; 404 means no matching route here. JSON parsing and other server failures are additional cases beyond this small route exercise.

For the exercise, implement handleRequest for /entries, validate before push, preserve saved records for later GET calls, and return 404 for /missing. The array is memory-only and disappears when the server stops. The browser checks your decision function; it does not launch Node or prove actual HTTP behavior. Download the supplied server and tests, install its declared packages locally, start it in one terminal, and run npm test in another to check the real routes.

title: A durable practice API
summary: Connect the API to a practice database and save entries.
explanation: Durable storage keeps data after a process stops. A JavaScript array is in memory and disappears on restart. A SQLite database opened with a file name stores records on disk. An adapter gives your code small methods such as save and load so callers can ask for storage without depending on its internal details. An adapter can be memory-only or durable; the method names alone do not prove persistence.

A prepared statement separates fixed SQL structure from the values supplied later. Placeholders such as ? stand for values, in order. The database handles their representation so a string value is not interpreted as extra SQL commands. Do not construct a query by concatenating untrusted input into its SQL text. Prepared statements address SQL input handling; range validation and ownership checks are still separate responsibilities.

Set membership helps compare ids. Suppose saved ids are {x, y} and requested ids are {x, z}. Their overlap is {x}, because only x occurs in both. z is requested but missing, and y is stored but not requested. Positions do not decide membership. A JavaScript Set stores distinct values and has(id) checks whether a particular id is present.

For the browser exercise, saveEntry must call store.save and loadEntries must call store.load. The supplied a and b rows must survive a later c addition. The browser adapter makes copied rows but does not write a disk file. The downloaded server uses practice.sqlite and prepared statements with the same storage idea. Save a record, stop and restart that local server in the same folder, and read it again; only that actual restart test establishes its durability.

analogy.connection: The notebook remains after you leave. A database record remains after the server stops.
analogy.limit: A database can still lose data if its file is deleted or its storage is temporary.

title: A reliable report API
summary: Use database queries to produce grouped reports and check missing values.
explanation: A report summarizes records instead of returning every original row. GROUP BY user_id makes a separate group for each user's sessions. COUNT(*) counts all records; COUNT(minutes) counts known durations; AVG(minutes) averages those known durations. A view stores a named query you can read like a table. It usually recalculates from underlying rows, rather than saving a frozen copy of the report.

Run this complete separate SQLite example:
```sql
CREATE TABLE demo_sessions (
  user_id TEXT,
  minutes INTEGER
);
INSERT INTO demo_sessions VALUES
  ('x', 12), ('x', 24), ('y', NULL), ('y', 18);
CREATE VIEW demo_report AS
SELECT user_id,
       COUNT(*) AS row_count,
       COUNT(minutes) AS known_count,
       AVG(minutes) AS average_minutes
FROM demo_sessions
GROUP BY user_id;
SELECT * FROM demo_report ORDER BY user_id;
```
The result is x: 2 rows, 2 known, average 18; y: 2 rows, 1 known, average 18. AS names each result column. SELECT * reads all the view's columns.

NULL means unknown, not zero. For durations 12, 24, NULL, the known-value average is (12 + 24) / 2 = 18, not 36 / 3 = 12. An all-NULL group has known_count 0 and average NULL. Showing the known count helps readers see how much evidence the average uses. One small report describes its supplied data; it does not prove what caused a change or what all users do.

A report can also include users with no sessions. Here is a second query, with a complete users schema, after the previous setup:
```sql
CREATE TABLE demo_users (
  id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT
);
INSERT INTO demo_users VALUES ('x', 'Nia'), ('y', 'Leo'), ('z', 'Uma');
SELECT u.id,
       COUNT(s.user_id) AS session_rows,
       COUNT(s.minutes) AS known_count,
       AVG(s.minutes) AS average_minutes
FROM demo_users AS u
LEFT JOIN demo_sessions AS s ON s.user_id = u.id
GROUP BY u.id
ORDER BY u.id;
```
User z has 0 session_rows, 0 known_count, and NULL average. COUNT(s.user_id) avoids counting the unmatched LEFT JOIN placeholder as a real session; COUNT(*) there would misleadingly count it as one row.

Joins can multiply rows when each session matches several records in another table. If a session with 10 minutes matches three tags, a later SUM could count its 10 three times. Before trusting an aggregate, inspect how many rows the join produces and what one result row represents. The exercise's query needs no join: it groups the sessions table directly.

For the exercise, replace the placeholder report view with a grouped query that returns user_id, row_count, known_count, and average_minutes. User a's 20 and 40 give row_count 2, known_count 2, average 30. User b has NULL and 10: row_count 2, known_count 1, average 10. Keep those column aliases and one result row per user; ORDER BY user_id helps display the report predictably.

The browser runs this SQL in an isolated SQLite database. A real report API also needs an HTTP route. In your downloaded SQLite server, a GET /report handler can execute the grouped query with db.prepare(...).all() and send res.json(rows); this is a description of integration, not a standalone executable snippet. The report should apply the project's permission rules when it contains private data. Compare the actual HTTP response with the expected two rows before calling that API complete.

title: A protected practice API
summary: Add request validation, authorization, middleware, and failure handling.
explanation: Authentication asks who is signed in. Authorization asks whether that person may act on a particular record. Validation asks whether the proposed values are acceptable. A protected update needs all three. Being signed in does not grant access to someone else's record, and owning a record does not make an invalid duration acceptable.

The order makes the write safe. Return before assignment whenever a requirement fails. A request body can claim ownerId: 'nora', but anyone can submit that text. The trusted identity must come from a server-verified session, then be compared with the record's stored owner. The permission helper accepts that verified result; it must not be treated as proof that an arbitrary supplied object really represents a signed-in person.

A session is a server-recognized sign-in state. In a real flow, the server verifies credentials, issues an unpredictable token, and checks that token and its expiry on later requests. A cookie can carry the token. The browser's claim to be a user is not trusted without that verification. Middleware runs before the route, validates the session, and attaches a trusted identity such as req.user; the route then performs record-specific authorization.

An Express middleware function typically receives req, res, and next. It either sends an error response and returns, or calls next() to continue to the route. Validation middleware can reject a malformed body before writing. A final error handler can report a useful failure without exposing private records, passwords, or internal credentials. Responses and logs must not reveal another user's data just to explain permission denial.

For the exercise, authorizeUpdate receives verified-session fixtures and mutates entry.minutes only after all checks pass. Null session returns 401; mismatched ownership returns 403; invalid minutes returns 400; a valid owner update returns 200 with entry. True AND false AND true is false: valid sign-in and input cannot overcome failed ownership. To finish actual protection locally, connect real session verification before using this helper; the next full-stack project supplies a localhost sign-in flow.

title: A complete private learning tracker
summary: Connect a front end, API, and database with sign-in and tested save flows.
explanation: A full-stack app connects a screen, an HTTP server, and durable storage. The screen sends a request. The server verifies the session, checks permissions and values, and writes permitted data. The screen then reads the saved result. A reload should read the database again, rather than rely on an old browser array. Each layer has a job, and a success message should reflect the server's actual result.

The local project stores entries in practice.sqlite with id, owner, and minutes columns. A prepared insert supplies the session's user as owner, not an owner from the body. A prepared SELECT with WHERE owner = ? reads only that session user's entries. Test as Alice, then Bob, to establish separation. Stopping and restarting clears memory sessions but should preserve database rows, so sign in again before checking persistence.

The supplied localhost login compares the chosen account's configured password, creates a random token with randomBytes, and stores its user and expiry in a server-side Map. The cookie carries that token. HttpOnly keeps page JavaScript from reading the cookie; SameSite=Strict limits when browsers attach it across sites; Max-Age sets a browser lifetime. The server still verifies its stored expiry. Environment variables supply passwords outside source code. Use your own throwaway local values and do not put them in repository files.

The learning server listens on 127.0.0.1, meaning only this computer's loopback address. It is deliberately a localhost exercise. Before a real public deployment, add HTTPS and Secure cookies, hashed password/account storage, login throttling, CSRF validation, and an established authentication library reviewed for your environment. CSRF means a different site trying to induce a signed-in browser to perform an unwanted action. The supplied sign-in is not a production authentication system.

Concurrent requests create another consistency risk. With a balance of 20, two requests can each read 20 and decide spending 15 is allowed. If they both rely on that stale read, the combined requested spending is 30, exceeding 20. A database transaction or atomic conditional update must check the current balance when each write happens. After one valid spend the balance is 5, so the next spend of 15 must fail. A memory-only function test does not prove this database concurrency protection.

For the exercise, amount must be a nonnegative integer no larger than available. A successful 7-unit move from available 20/saved 0 returns 13/7 and preserves 20. A forced failure, negative amount, or overspend returns the old values in a copy. Then test the downloaded app separately: sign in, save valid minutes, reload, reject invalid input, check two-user separation, and check restart persistence. The browser checks the transfer invariant; the actual screen, HTTP, storage, and session behavior need their own local evidence.

analogy.familiar: Writing a score and checking the scoreboard
analogy.connection: After a successful write, the scoreboard should show the same saved value when you look again.
analogy.limit: A screen’s optimistic number is not proof the server saved it.

steps: Implement transfer(state,amount,fail=false) using the supplied state {available:20,saved:0}.

Download the local app files. Set different ALICE_PASSWORD and BOB_PASSWORD values in your terminal without putting them in source files. Run npm install then npm start.
Open the local app, sign in as alice, save an entry and reload. Sign in as bob and verify alice’s entry is absent. Restart the server, sign in again, and check saved entries remain.

function transfer(state,amount,fail=false){return {...state};}
console.log(transfer({available:20,saved:0},7));
solution:
function transfer(state,amount,fail=false){if(fail||!Number.isInteger(amount)||amount<0||amount>state.available)return {...state};return {available:state.available-amount,saved:state.saved+amount};}
console.log(transfer({available:20,saved:0},7));

quiz.explanation: The displayed saved state should match the server result. A failed request needs a clear message and a safe retry.

Subtract amount from available and add the same amount to saved.

math.explanation: A consistency invariant is something that must stay true after every allowed change. Here available + saved must stay 20.

math.feedback: Both can read the old balance 20 before either writes. A database transaction or atomic conditional update must check the current balance when applying each change.

title: A clean starter project
summary: Create a small project with named files and a clear entry point.
explanation: A project is a folder containing files that belong together. A clear entry point tells you which file starts the program. For this project it is main.js. A README is a note explaining what the project does and how to run it. File names and paths matter: a computer does not guess that main.js and main.txt were meant to be the same file.

A code editor lets you change and save files. .js identifies JavaScript source. .md identifies Markdown text, often used for notes. A folder name organizes files but is not itself the program. Save the code before running it: the runtime reads the saved file, so an unsaved editor change may not be what executes.

To try the example locally, create a new folder called greeting-demo and save the example as main.js there. With Node.js installed, run these commands from that folder's parent on macOS:
```bash
cd greeting-demo
ls
node main.js
```
cd changes the current folder; ls lists its files so you can confirm main.js is there; node main.js asks Node to execute that file. You should see the same greeting once. Node is a JavaScript runtime outside the browser. The terminal command is not JavaScript to paste into main.js.

A useful README states the entry point, runtime requirement, launch command, and expected output. Here is example README content, shown as plain text rather than executable code:
```text
Greeting demo
Entry point: main.js
Runtime: Node.js 22.13 or newer
Run from this folder: node main.js
Expected output: Let us build something!
```
Opening README.md lets you read the instructions; executing main.js runs the program. Keeping both files in the same folder makes the project easier to carry to another computer.

For the exercise, set message to exactly Ready to build! and log it once. Capitalization and the exclamation mark are part of the requested output. Repeated console.log calls would produce extra lines. The app's Run action executes your lesson code; it does not automatically create a folder on your computer.

Download main.js and the supplied README.md into your new hello-project folder and open both in your own editor. Check the app's saved-file status before downloading, then verify the downloaded main.js actually contains the current code. If Node is installed, launch it locally and compare the single output line with the README. This completes both the browser exercise and the project-structure practice.

title: Repair a broken starter
summary: Find one supplied error, make a small change, and run the project again.
explanation: Debugging means finding why actual behavior differs from expected behavior. Start with a small reproducible input and a clear expected result. An error message or unexpected output is evidence about what the program did. Keep the input fixed while making a focused change, then compare again so you can tell what the change accomplished.

A logic error produces incorrect behavior despite readable syntax. A syntax error means the code cannot be read as a valid program, such as an unmatched parenthesis. A runtime error occurs while executing, such as calling a missing function. These are different kinds of clues. Changing unrelated formatting will not fix a wrong arithmetic operator.

A small debugging loop is: predict, run, inspect, change, rerun. When an error mentions a file and line, read that location and the nearby code; sometimes the real cause begins earlier, such as a missing closing bracket. Use the smallest change that explains the evidence. If a fix changes the expected behavior elsewhere, investigate that difference rather than hiding its output.

For the exercise, total(a, b) should add its two numeric inputs. The starter subtracts. Change that operation and preserve the general function, rather than returning the literal 11 for every call. The supplied cases include 4 + 7 = 11, 0 + 7 = 7, and -2 + 5 = 3. A hard-coded answer could pass one case and fail the others.

The condition total(4, 7) === 11 becomes true after the correction, because both sides are the same number. It is a comparison result, not the text 'total'. These fixture inputs are numbers; if a future caller supplies strings, JavaScript's + can join text instead of adding. Define and validate inputs when extending the function rather than assuming every call is numeric.

analogy.familiar: Checking a receipt total
analogy.connection: If the total looks wrong, compare it with the listed items and find the first calculation that differs.
analogy.limit: A running program can still produce an incorrect result.

steps: Run the starter with inputs 4 and 7. Notice the printed result is -3 instead of 11.
Find the operator inside total and replace it with the operator for addition.
Run again. Then check 0 plus 7 and -2 plus 5.

console.log(total(4,7));
solution:

console.log(total(4,7));

quiz.explanation: Its syntax is valid, but the chosen operation does not match the intended behavior.

math.question: After the fix, is total(4,7) === 11 true?
math.feedback: 4 + 7 is 11, so comparing that result with 11 gives true.

title: A project you can launch
summary: Move into a supplied project folder and run its documented start command.
explanation: A terminal lets you run programs by typing commands. It always has a current working folder. Relative paths start from that folder: node main.js looks for main.js there. A 'cannot find' message can mean you are in the wrong folder, not that a file was deleted. Check your location before changing the code.

Here is a macOS terminal walkthrough. First create a new launch-demo folder containing main.js with console.log('Launched the demo'); and the package.json from the next page. Begin in that folder's parent:
```bash

```
pwd prints the current folder; ls lists files; cd enters launch-demo. After cd, ls should show main.js and package.json. npm start should print Launched the demo, possibly with npm's own script banner. You need Node and npm installed for the final command.

npm start reads scripts.start and executes its stored command. In this example that command is node main.js. It runs from the project context, where the relative file exists. A different downloaded project may run a build tool or server instead, so read its scripts and instructions before running them. npm is the package manager and script runner; Node is the JavaScript runtime.

For the exercise, use exactly two strings in order: cd hello-project, then npm start. The cd step comes first because the starting location is the parent folder. title: A project with version history
summary: Save two meaningful commits and restore a deliberately broken change.
explanation: Git records versions you choose to save. A commit is a saved snapshot with a message explaining the change. Your working files can contain edits that are not committed. Staging selects the changes for the next commit; committing records that selection. Git does not automatically save every edit, and a local commit does not publish anything.

Use a disposable new folder called history-demo. Put a main.js file there that prints Hello. From its parent, this terminal sequence creates local history. Git must be installed, and the example identity is only for this disposable repository:
```bash
cd history-demo
git init
git config user.name "Practice Learner"
git config user.email "learner@example.invalid"
git status
git add main.js
git commit -m "Add greeting"
```
init creates a repository; local config supplies an author identity; status shows file state. add stages main.js, and commit records that staged version with the supplied message.

Now edit main.js in your editor so it prints Hello, reader and save it. Run it to confirm the greeting, then use:
```bash
git diff
git add main.js
git commit -m "Improve greeting"
git log --oneline -2
```
diff shows unstaged changes. The second commit saves the improvement. log --oneline -2 shows the newest two commits as short identifiers and messages. Staging is a step before the commit; it does not delete old history.

For recovery practice, deliberately change that greeting to broken in this disposable file and save it. First inspect the difference and copy any uncommitted work you want to keep outside the file. Then run:
```bash
git status
git diff
git restore --source=HEAD -- main.js
node main.js
```
HEAD means the current commit. restore replaces this uncommitted file with HEAD's version; -- separates the file path from options. The program prints Hello, reader again. This discards the selected file's uncommitted change, so preserve wanted edits before restoring.

A committed mistake needs a different recovery. git revert with the mistake's commit id creates a new commit reversing it, preserving history. For example, in a disposable repository where the newest commit is the mistake, git revert HEAD reverses that commit and records the reversal. Review the chosen commit first; an older change can conflict with later work. Avoid destructive reset commands while learning this workflow.

For the exercise, restore returns a copy of the last versions entry. The supplied history has two entries, so the latest code is Hello, coder and the original first entry remains Hello. The function assumes a nonempty history, as supplied. Finish the local Git task as well: inspect two meaningful commits, recover one uncommitted mistake, and rerun the restored program. The browser model cannot establish that real Git history exists on your computer.

analogy.familiar: Keeping dated versions of an assignment
analogy.connection: You can compare the versions and return to a known working one.
analogy.limit: Git only records the files and changes you intentionally add to a commit.

steps: Complete restore(history) so it returns a copy of the most recent saved version, not the broken working copy.

title: A reproducible project
summary: Declare dependencies and write instructions for running the project.
explanation: A reproducible project can be started from a clean copy using written instructions. A dependency is a package the code uses. package.json describes the project, needed packages, and runnable scripts. A lockfile, usually package-lock.json for npm, records the exact resolved package versions. Those are different jobs: a version range allows choices; the lockfile records the choices actually made.

Create main.js in the same disposable repro-demo folder with console.log('Clean start works');. Use these commands from the folder:
```bash
node --version
npm install
npm start
npm ci
npm start
```
The version check reports your runtime. install reads the manifest and creates or updates the lockfile when needed. start prints Clean start works. Once a matching lockfile exists, ci performs a clean installation using its recorded dependency versions, then the second start should work too. ci replaces node_modules, so use a clean practice copy for this walkthrough.

npm install and npm ci are not interchangeable in every situation. ci needs an existing lockfile that agrees with package.json; it fails instead of silently changing an inconsistent lockfile. Keep the manifest and lockfile in project history. node_modules contains installed package files and can usually be recreated. A lockfile improves consistency but does not promise identical behavior across every operating system or runtime version.

A README should tell another person the runtime requirement, setup command, launch command, and expected behavior. Here is plain example content, not a program:
```text
Repro demo
Requires Node.js 22.13 or newer.
Initial setup: npm install
Keep the generated package-lock.json.
Clean-copy setup with that lockfile: npm ci
Launch: npm start
Expected output: Clean start works
Third-party runtime dependencies: none
```
Test these instructions on a fresh copy so missing steps become visible. A screenshot of a successful run cannot replace the saved dependency information.

The browser exercise represents package settings in a JavaScript object named project. Set scripts.start to node main.js and engines.node to >=22.13.0. Keep dependencies empty because no third-party runtime package is used. Object.keys(project.dependencies) gives an array of its property names; length 0 establishes there are no declared dependencies. A JavaScript object literal may use single quotes, but a real JSON file requires double quotes.

After the declaration passes, download the supplied files and follow the README locally. Confirm both the initial install and a clean-copy install with its saved lockfile, then start the program. The browser checks the declaration, not package installation. Read scripts before running someone else's project, and declare only packages it actually needs; invented dependencies create extra setup and review work without helping this program.

analogy.familiar: A recipe’s ingredient list and instructions
analogy.connection: The package file lists what the project needs, and the README explains how to put it together.
analogy.limit: A package may run installation scripts; use a trusted registry and review what you add.

title: A reviewed AI change
summary: Describe a small feature, review an AI proposal, apply it, and check the result.
explanation: An AI coding proposal is a proposed change you need to understand and verify. Describe the promised behavior with examples before reviewing it: who should get a discount, how much, and what happens for invalid input. A confident explanation is not proof that code satisfies those requirements. Read the changed lines, then check the behavior that matters.

Validation should happen before the calculation. Number.isFinite checks that price is an actual finite number; it rejects NaN, Infinity, and numeric text. price < 0 rejects a negative number, while 0 is valid. Membership must be the boolean true, not merely a truthy value. Nonempty strings such as 'false' are truthy in JavaScript, so if(isMember) alone can accidentally grant them a discount.

For the exercise, the discount is ten percent rather than this walkthrough's twenty percent. Ten percent of 80 is 8, so a member keeps 80 - 8 = 72, equivalent to 80 × 0.9. A nonmember keeps 80. Validate the price first, then choose the member calculation. isMember === true prevents a string from receiving the discount. Invalid negative, NaN, or Infinity prices return null.

Review meaningful cases: valid member, valid nonmember, zero, negative, non-finite value, and a truthy string posing as membership. Keep the earlier working code in History or Git so you can recover if the proposal breaks a promised behavior. Explain why each branch exists before accepting it. For real money, fractional representation and rounding rules also need explicit decisions; this small number exercise checks the supplied arithmetic rule.

Implement finalPrice with the supplied names and confirm all relevant checks. An AI that changes only the first example might still get the nonmember case wrong. Ask for a focused explanation or hint when a line is unclear, then inspect and test it yourself. If a new change causes a regression, restore the known working version while investigating instead of treating the AI's reassurance as evidence.

analogy.familiar: Checking someone else’s homework steps
analogy.connection: A useful suggestion still needs you to follow the steps and check the result.
analogy.limit: The assistant can make mistakes even when the explanation sounds confident.

steps: Implement finalPrice(price,isMember): return null for non-finite or negative prices.
Apply a ten-percent discount only when isMember is true; otherwise return the original price.

console.log(finalPrice(100,false));
solution:
function finalPrice(price,isMember){if(!Number.isFinite(price)||price<0)return null;return isMember===true?price*0.9:price;}
console.log(finalPrice(100,false));

title: A tested feature
summary: Check normal, empty, boundary, failure, and concurrency cases where applicable.
explanation: A useful test checks promised behavior by comparing actual and expected results. It should fail when that behavior breaks. For clamping, a valid number below the range becomes the lower limit, one above becomes the upper limit, and one already inside stays unchanged. First reject the wrong kind of input; then apply the boundaries.

Run the test locally with Node installed:
```bash
node --test test-level.mjs
```
Passing assertions produce a passing test report. The module's demonstration console logs may also appear because importing evaluates that module. Temporarily replace the clamp with return value and rerun: outside-range assertions should fail. Restore the working code afterward. A test that only confirms the function exists would not catch that broken behavior.

Choose cases from the feature's requirements. Normal input verifies ordinary use; boundaries verify the exact included endpoints; just-outside values verify the transition; invalid input verifies rejection. Empty input can mean undefined here rather than a zero-length list. Concurrency tests are useful for shared balance updates, but this pure calculation has no shared mutable state, so concurrency is not a relevant risk for it.

For clampScore, use the exercise's 0-through-100 limits and preserve null for non-integers. Check 42, 0, 100, -5, and 110, plus undefined, NaN, Infinity, and 2.5. The inside result 100 and the just-outside result for 101 are both 100, but for different reasons: the first is already valid; the second must be clamped. Together they test the boundary transition.

The browser checks your function's behavior. Download score.mjs and test.mjs, replace the supplied score stub with your implementation, and run node --test test.mjs from their folder. A working browser function does not automatically edit that local stub. Break a relevant behavior briefly and confirm the local test fails, then restore and rerun. Passing tests are evidence for their stated cases, not proof of every possible property.

analogy.familiar: Trying a door from both sides and checking its latch
analogy.connection: Several meaningful checks tell you more than looking at the door once.
analogy.limit: More tests do not guarantee correctness if all tests miss the same important behavior.

steps: Implement clampScore: return null unless input is a finite integer.
Keep valid whole numbers within 0..100 using a lower and upper boundary.
Add cases for 42, 0, 100, -5, 110, undefined, NaN, Infinity, and 2.5.
Run the supplied downloadable Node test after replacing its stub with your solution. Break the function briefly and confirm a relevant test fails.
starter:
function clampScore(value){return value;}
console.log(clampScore(110));
solution:
function clampScore(value){if(!Number.isInteger(value))return null;return Math.max(0,Math.min(100,value));}
console.log(clampScore(110));

checks.label: Outside values clamp to the nearest limit

math.question: Why test both 100 and 101?
choices: To check the included boundary and the value immediately outside it

title: A maintainable published app
summary: Deploy a small app, check its health, and reproduce a failure using useful logs.
explanation: Deployment makes a particular built version available to its intended users. Record a release identifier so you can tell which version is served and which previous version to restore. A successful local run proves only the local run. After deployment, check a response from the actual published app for the expected version and behavior.

A macOS terminal can start that disposable local server with a deliberate storage failure:
```bash
RELEASE_ID=demo-4 STORAGE_READY=false node health-server.mjs
```
While it runs, use another terminal:
```bash
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:3030/health
```
-i includes response headers. Expect 503 and version demo-4. Stop the server with Control-C, restart with STORAGE_READY=true, and request again; expect 200. This flag simulates readiness, so it does not actually probe a database or prove all screens work.

Logs are recorded events that help investigate problems. A useful failure record might contain requestId, releaseId, and a category such as storage-unavailable. Match an observed failure to its log using the request id. Avoid logging passwords, keys, or private message content. Reproduce a failure in a disposable local test before guessing at a fix. Observability means having enough useful evidence to understand what the running app is doing.

Before release, run relevant checks, confirm the intended audience, and identify the previous working version. Record that evidence and your hosting provider's restore procedure in RELEASE.md. Rollback returns the served app to that working version; saved-data changes may need separate backup or migration recovery. Practice restoration in a private test environment and check its actual version afterward.

For the exercise, health(appReady, storageReady, version) returns numeric 200 only when both conditions are ready, otherwise 503, and includes version either way. The browser checks this decision function; Run performs no deployment. The supplied local server demonstrates a readiness flag and version, not every dependency. Actual hosting, health verification, and rollback are separate tasks in your chosen private provider project and may involve account or usage costs. Follow that provider's instructions and verify the real served release.

analogy.limit: A health check is limited evidence; it does not test every screen or behavior.

title: A reviewed release
summary: Review permissions, secrets, input handling, dependency risks, and keyboard access.
explanation: A release review compares requirements with actual evidence. Check record permissions, secret handling, input validation, safe output, dependencies, and keyboard access. A checked box without a real observation proves little. Record findings, fixes, and remaining limits so someone reading the review can understand what was verified.

Displaying untrusted text safely matters. This complete browser HTML example uses textContent: ```html Safe text demo

``` The paragraph shows the literal characters Hello. textContent treats the string as text. innerHTML would interpret the tags as markup. eval would interpret suitable text as JavaScript. Use a reviewed sanitizer when a feature truly requires supplied HTML.

Server validation checks input shape, size, and allowed ranges before a write. Permission tests should use two users and attempt access to another user's records. Keep secrets outside browser code, repository history, and logs: anything shipped to the browser can be read by its user. Dependency review compares declared packages and shipped versions with current advisories; a past clean report may be stale.

Accessibility review checks whether people can identify and use controls. Inputs need meaningful labels, keyboard focus should be visible, Tab order should follow the task, and errors should explain what to fix. This complete HTML example supplies a label and native keyboard-accessible button:
```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Label demo</title></head>
<body>
  <form>
    <label for="minutes">Practice minutes</label>
    <input id="minutes" type="number" min="1" max="180" required>
    <button type="submit">Save practice</button>
  </form>
</body>
</html>
```
Tab reaches the field and then the button. The label's for matches the input id. Browser number bounds assist input but do not replace server validation. This page has no save server, so it demonstrates labeling and keyboard controls rather than persistence.

Three independent true/false requirements create 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 combinations. Only true/true/true passes, so there is one allowed combination. One missing or false requirement is enough to fail. A truthy string is not a completed review; strict comparison prevents 'true' from being treated as evidence. The function assumes it receives a review object; validating an entirely missing argument would be an additional input contract.

For canRelease, check permissionChecks, secretChecks, and keyboardChecks with === true, joined by &&. Then use the supplied REVIEW.md against a real private project: test account separation, inspect shipped code and logs for secrets, try invalid and oversized input, inspect dependencies, and complete the core task with keyboard alone. Include safe output, labels, errors, and recoverability. The browser verifies your decision function; it cannot establish the real project's security or accessibility review.

analogy.familiar: Checking an assignment against its stated requirements

steps: Implement canRelease(review) so permissionChecks, secretChecks, and keyboardChecks must all be true booleans.
Do not accept missing values or the string "true" as a passed review.
Run cases where one requirement is false or missing.
Use the supplied checklist against a real private project: test another user’s records, inspect the browser bundle for secrets, and use the app entirely by keyboard.
Record findings, evidence, fixes, and unresolved limits before you decide to release.

function canRelease(review){return !!review.permissionChecks;}
console.log(canRelease({permissionChecks:true,secretChecks:false,keyboardChecks:true}));

function canRelease(review){return review.permissionChecks===true&&review.secretChecks===true&&review.keyboardChecks===true;}
console.log(canRelease({permissionChecks:true,secretChecks:false,keyboardChecks:true}));

# Private release review

For each item record evidence and unresolved limits.
- Account and record permissions: test two users.
- Secrets: inspect browser bundle, repository and logs.
- Input: normal, invalid, boundary, oversized values.
- Output: untrusted text is displayed safely.
- Dependencies: inspect declared packages and current advisories.
- Keyboard: every core action reachable; focus visible.
- Labels and errors: inputs and feedback understandable.
- Recoverability: test previous version and saved-data backup.

Release decision: record after actual checks.

externalNotes: The browser checks the release decision function. A real security and accessibility review requires the specific project and current dependency information; fill the checklist with actual evidence.
